courseDescription: A rigorous, calculus-based introduction to classical mechanics designed for students with a foundation in mathematics. This course covers kinematics, Newton's laws, energy, momentum, rotational dynamics, oscillations, and gravitation, providing a comprehensive framework for understanding the physical world through both conceptual intuition and formal mathematical derivation.
targetLearner: Students comfortable with differential and integral calculus who seek a systematic and deep understanding of classical physical laws.

projects.project_name: Computational Orbital Mechanic: Simulating a Moon Mission
projects.project_description: In this project, you will build a physics-based simulation of a spacecraft traveling from Earth to the Moon. You will progressively develop a numerical engine that calculates trajectories, handles engine burns using energy principles, manages angular momentum during maneuvers, and finally accounts for lunar gravity to achieve orbit.
projects.final_deliverable: A comprehensive Python script (or spreadsheet model) containing a multi-stage numerical integrator that predicts the spacecraft's 2D position and velocity vectors over time, including energy and momentum verification plots and a successful lunar orbit insertion.

units.title: Describing Motion
units.description: This unit establishes the mathematical language of physics. You will learn to use vectors to describe position, velocity, and acceleration in one and two dimensions, including projectile and circular motion.

lectures.title: Measurement and Vectors
lectures.description: Foundational tools for physical analysis, focusing on how we quantify the universe and represent directional quantities mathematically.

sessions.title: Units and Dimensions
sessions.description: This session introduces the SI system and dimensional analysis techniques used to verify physical equations. You will learn to perform unit conversions and check for dimensional consistency, ensuring you can build mathematically sound models as you progress through more complex physics topics.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the lecture by reframing physics not as a collection of formulas, but as a quantitative language for describing the universe. The core mission today is to establish the 'alphabet' of this language: the SI units. Explain that while any unit is arbitrary, consistency is the bedrock of science. Use the concept of 'standard candles' to explain why we use the meter, kilogram, and second as our primary base units. Emphasize that every physical quantity—no matter how complex—is just a combination of these base dimensions. This is the first step in moving the student from intuitive guessing to rigorous modeling.

Introduce the 'Chain-Link' method for unit conversion. This is a critical technical skill designed to prevent the common mistake of multiplying when one should divide. Visualize this on the whiteboard as a series of fractions where units are treated like algebraic variables that can be canceled out. Instead of just showing the conversion of miles per hour to meters per second, walk through the logic of 'eliminating' the unwanted unit (miles) by placing it in the denominator of a conversion factor, and then doing the same for hours. This technique ensures that the learner's final answer isn't just a number, but a meaningful physical measurement.

Transition to Dimensional Analysis by asking a fundamental question: 'How do we know if an equation is even possible?' Explain that for an equation to be valid, the dimensions on both sides must be identical—you cannot add apples to oranges, and in physics, you cannot add a velocity to an acceleration. Use the whiteboard to break down complex units like the Newton (Force) into its base components (kg·m/s²). This 'deconstruction' is a powerful diagnostic tool. By analyzing the dimensions of a constant like the Gravitational constant (G), show learners that the units of constants are often derived purely to make the rest of the equation's dimensions balance out.

Conclude by demonstrating a 'Sanity Check' using the kinematic equation v² = 2ax. Rather than solving for a variable, lead the class through a dimensional check where [L/T]² is compared against [L/T²] * [L]. This reveals the 'DNA' of the equation. Explain that if the dimensions don't match, the physics is wrong, regardless of the numbers used. This practice moment is designed to instill a habit of self-correction; if a student forgets a square root or a factor of 't' in a later exam, their knowledge of dimensional consistency will be their primary safety net.

tasks: Convert 60 miles per hour to meters per second using chain-link conversion.
Determine the dimensions of the constant G in Newton's Law of Gravitation given F = GmM/r^2.
Use dimensional analysis to determine if the equation v^2 = 2ax is dimensionally consistent.

sessions.title: Estimation and Significant Figures
sessions.description: This session teaches you how to manage uncertainty in measurements through significant figure rules and order-of-magnitude estimation. You will gain the ability to provide realistic physical estimates, a crucial skill for the initial 'sanity check' phase of your course project's kinematic modeling.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the common misconception that more digits in a number imply higher quality data. In a 'concept-first' public lecture style, we begin by framing physics not just as the study of laws, but as the art of measurement. I will illustrate that every number we write down carries a silent promise of precision. If we say a car is moving at 60 mph, does that mean 60.000 or somewhere between 55 and 65? This leads directly into the 'why' of Significant Figures: they are our way of being honest about the limitations of our tools. We will visualize a ruler with only centimeter markings to demonstrate why the last digit in any measurement is always an 'estimated' digit, yet still significant.

Transition into the formal rules of Significant Figures by treating them as a language of reliability. Instead of just listing rules for zeros, we will group them by their 'job': placeholder zeros versus measurement zeros. I'll use the example of 0.004567 to show that leading zeros are merely 'pointing' to the decimal place, while the digits 4, 5, 6, and 7 are the ones actually doing the work of measuring. To prevent the common error of over-precision in calculations, we will work through the rectangle area problem. The logic here is that the final result cannot be 'sturdier' than its weakest link; if one side is measured to only two digits of precision (5.6 cm), reporting an area with four decimal places is a physical lie. We must round the result to match the least precise input.

Shift the focus from precision to scale with the introduction of Order-of-Magnitude estimation and Fermi problems. This is the 'sanity check' phase essential for any physicist. I will pose the classic question about piano tuners in a large city to demonstrate how we can arrive at a remarkably accurate ballpark figure using only logical guesses and powers of ten. The goal is to move students away from the fear of being 'wrong' and toward the confidence of being 'roughly right.' We break the problem down: How many people live in a house? How many houses have a piano? How often is a piano tuned? By multiplying these rough estimates, we show that a complex social or physical system can be modeled on the back of an envelope.

Conclude by connecting these two concepts—precision and estimation—to the upcoming course project. Explain that while significant figures ensure our mathematical models are rigorous, order-of-magnitude estimates allow us to detect major errors before we even touch a calculator. I'll demonstrate this by rounding 0.004567 to two significant figures (0.0046), emphasizing that we are retaining the 'spirit' of the measurement while discarding the noise. This session builds the instinctive habit of looking at a calculated result and asking, 'Does this scale make sense, and have I claimed more knowledge than my measurements allow?'

tasks: Calculate the area of a rectangle with sides 12.34 cm and 5.6 cm, expressing the result with the correct significant figures.
Perform a Fermi estimate of the number of piano tuners in a city of 1 million people.
Round the number 0.004567 to two significant figures.

sessions.title: Vectors and Components
sessions.description: This session covers the decomposition of vector quantities into orthogonal components using trigonometry. You will learn to translate a vector's magnitude and direction into (x, y) coordinates, providing the essential mathematical bridge between physical intuition and algebraic calculation.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by bridging the gap between everyday experience and mathematical abstraction. In the previous sessions, we discussed quantities like temperature or mass (scalars), which only need a number. Now, shift the focus to 'directional' quantities. On the whiteboard, draw a simple arrow representing a person walking 5 meters. Ask the question: 'Does it matter which way they walk?' This introduces the vector as an entity possessing both magnitude and direction. The key objective here is to move away from treating vectors as just 'arrows' and start treating them as manageable mathematical objects. Emphasize that in physics, we often cannot solve problems with diagonal lines; we need to align everything to a grid.

Introduce the concept of 'Orthogonal Decomposition.' Explain that any diagonal vector is essentially a combination of a horizontal 'shadow' and a vertical 'shadow.' Use the whiteboard to draw a vector in the first quadrant of a Cartesian plane. Label the angle $\theta$ measured from the positive x-axis. This is a critical moment: derive the components $Ax = A \cos(\theta)$ and $Ay = A \sin(\theta)$. Explain that the 'why' behind this is the definition of sine and cosine in a right-angled triangle. A common pitfall for students is blindly using cosine for 'x' and sine for 'y'; correct this by showing a scenario where the angle is measured from the y-axis, demonstrating that the 'adjacent' side determines the cosine, not the axis itself.

Transition to the 'Inverse Problem': recovering the vector's magnitude and direction from its components. Show that if we know how far right and how far up we've gone, the Pythagorean theorem ($A = \sqrt{Ax^2 + Ay^2}$) tells us the total distance, and the inverse tangent ($\tan^{-1}(Ay/Ax)$) gives us the direction. This is where you must address the 'Quadrant Trap.' When students calculate $\tan^{-1}$ on a calculator for a vector in the second or third quadrant, the calculator often gives an ambiguous or 'incorrect' angle relative to the standard orientation. Use a whiteboard example like the vector $(-3, 4)$ to show that while the math might suggest a certain angle, a quick sketch reveals the vector is actually in the second quadrant, requiring an adjustment of 180 degrees.

Conclude by applying these concepts to a real-world displacement scenario, such as a hiker traveling 5m at a bearing of 225 degrees. This specific angle is useful because it forces students to work in the third quadrant where both components are negative. Have the students calculate these components as a check for understanding. This exercise reveals whether they understand that the 'sign' of the component indicates direction (left/right, up/down). Reinforce that these components are the 'DNA' of the vector—once we have them, we can add, subtract, and multiply vectors with ease in the next session.

tasks: A vector has a magnitude of 10 and an angle of 30 degrees from the x-axis; find its x and y components.
Convert the vector (-3, 4) from component form to magnitude-direction form.
Draw a vector representing a displacement of 5m at 225 degrees and calculate its components.

sessions.title: Vector Addition and Products
sessions.description: This session introduces vector algebra, including tip-to-tail addition and the definitions of dot and cross products. You will master the operations needed to manipulate multiple forces and velocities, which is a prerequisite for analyzing multi-dimensional systems in Unit 2.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by transitioning from static vector representation to dynamic vector manipulation. The core idea here is that in physics, quantities like force and velocity rarely act in isolation; understanding how they combine is the fundamental prerequisite for Newton’s Laws. We start with the tip-to-tail method, visualizing vector addition as a 'journey' where the resultant vector is the net displacement. On the whiteboard, draw two vectors, A and B, in different quadrants. The teacher should emphasize that while the graphical method provides an intuitive 'feel' for the direction of the result, the analytical method—adding corresponding components—is the rigorous tool we use for calculation. We must explicitly point out that you cannot simply add magnitudes unless the vectors are parallel; this is a common trap for students transitioning from scalar algebra.

After mastering addition, we introduce the concept of the 'product' of two vectors, starting with the Dot Product (Scalar Product). To make this concept-first, explain the dot product as a measure of how much one vector 'projects' onto another. It is a scalar—a single number representing alignment. On the board, derive the formula A · B = AB cos(θ) alongside the component-wise sum (AxBx + AyBy). The key takeaway here is that the dot product is maximized when vectors are parallel and zero when they are orthogonal. This isn't just a math trick; it's the mathematical foundation for 'Work' in Unit 3, where only the force component in the direction of motion matters.

We then move to the more complex Cross Product (Vector Product). Unlike the dot product, the result here is a new vector, representing an area or a 'rotational' influence. This is often the most abstract part of the lecture. Visualize the cross product as constructing a parallelogram from two vectors, where the magnitude of the product is the area of that shape. Explain that the direction of this new vector must be perpendicular to the plane formed by the original two. To help students internalize this, introduce the Right-Hand Rule as a physical mnemonic. The teacher should physically demonstrate the gesture: fingers curling from the first vector to the second, thumb pointing toward the result. This prepares them for the later complexities of torque and angular momentum.

To wrap up, we engage in a practice check where we add A=(2,3) and B=(-1,4). This serves to solidify the ease of component addition. We then compute a 3D dot product to show that the principle holds across any number of dimensions. Finally, we pose a challenge: if two vectors lie entirely in the xy-plane, where must their cross product point? This question is designed to reveal if the learner understands that cross products always exit the plane of the operands, a crucial realization for understanding the z-axis in a 2D-focused coordinate system. This session provides the algebraic 'engine' that will power every dynamic model they build in the course project.

tasks: Add vectors A=(2,3) and B=(-1,4) analytically.
Calculate the dot product of A=(1,2,0) and B=(3,-1,5).
Determine the direction of the cross product of two vectors in the xy-plane using the right-hand rule.

lectures.title: Motion in One Dimension
lectures.description: A rigorous look at linear motion, defining the relationships between displacement, velocity, and acceleration through calculus.

sessions.title: Position, Displacement, and Velocity
sessions.description: This session defines the rate of change of position, distinguishing between average and instantaneous velocity using the limit definition of a derivative. You will understand how to interpret motion through x-t graphs, which is the first step in describing the trajectory of any mechanical system.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by grounding the abstract concept of motion in the physical reality of a coordinate system. Explain that physics begins not with math, but with an agreement on where 'zero' is and which direction counts as positive. Introduce the position vector as a 'pointer' from the origin to the object. The crucial distinction to make here is between distance—the total ground covered—and displacement, which is the net change in position. To make this intuitive, use the example of a runner returning to the starting line: their distance is great, but their displacement is zero. This sets the stage for why we need more precise tools than just 'speed' to describe mechanics.

Transition to the visual representation of motion through the position-time (x-t) graph. Instead of just plotting points, guide the learners to see the slope as a physical story. A steep slope means 'fast,' a flat line means 'at rest,' and a negative slope means 'coming home.' Address a common misconception early: students often confuse the height of the graph (where the object is) with the steepness of the graph (how fast it is moving). By emphasizing that the graph's 'steepness' is the physical manifestation of velocity, you bridge the gap between geometry and physics.

Now, introduce the formal definition of velocity through the lens of calculus, catering to the 'concept-first' lecture style. Start with Average Velocity as the slope of a secant line between two points. Then, pose a philosophical question: 'How fast is the object moving at exactly one moment in time?' This leads naturally to the limit definition of the derivative. Show that as the time interval shrinks to zero, the secant line becomes a tangent line. This is the 'aha!' moment where the derivative is no longer just a math rule from a textbook, but the physical reality of instantaneous motion. Use the function x(t) = 3t^2 + 2t to demonstrate this; show how the power rule provides a velocity function v(t) = 6t + 2, allowing us to 'peek' at the object's speed at exactly t=2s.

Conclude by challenging the learners with a scenario where speed is constant but velocity might not be, or where average velocity is zero despite high-speed movement in between. This reinforces the vector nature of velocity. Use a practice prompt regarding a trip with varying speeds to reveal if learners are simply averaging numbers (a common error) or if they understand that average velocity must be calculated as total displacement over total time. This distinction is vital for the upcoming sessions on acceleration, as it ensures they are thinking about the net change in the system rather than just the immediate sensation of motion.

tasks: Given x(t) = 3t^2 + 2t, find the instantaneous velocity at t=2s.
Interpret a position-time graph to determine when an object is at rest or moving backward.
Calculate average velocity for a trip where speeds vary over different time intervals.

sessions.title: Acceleration
sessions.description: This session introduces acceleration as the second derivative of position. You will learn to relate the slope of a v-t graph to physical speeding up or slowing down, allowing you to predict how velocities change over time in your project simulations.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by bridging the gap from the previous session's discussion on velocity. Introduce acceleration not just as 'speeding up,' but as the rigorous mathematical rate at which velocity changes. Use the whiteboard to write the definition of instantaneous acceleration as the derivative of velocity with respect to time, which consequently establishes it as the second derivative of position. The key takeaway here is the hierarchy of motion: position tells us where we are, velocity tells us how we are moving, and acceleration tells us how that movement itself is evolving. Emphasize that in physics, a 'change' in velocity includes changes in magnitude or direction, though we focus on magnitude in this 1D context.

Transition to a visual analysis using velocity-time (v-t) graphs. Draw a curve on the board and demonstrate that the slope at any single point is the instantaneous acceleration. This is a crucial conceptual hurdle; students often confuse the value of the function (the velocity) with its slope (the acceleration). Use a specific scenario: a car moving in the negative direction but braking. Show that even though the velocity is negative, the slope of the v-t graph is positive. This helps prevent the common misconception that 'negative acceleration' always means 'slowing down.' Explain that if velocity and acceleration share the same sign, the object speeds up; if they have opposite signs, it slows down.

Work through a symbolic example on the board, such as v(t) = 5t^3, to derive a(t) = 15t^2. This reinforces the power of the power rule in calculus and shows that acceleration itself can be a function of time, not just a constant. Ask the students to consider what the units of this result mean—meters per second, per second (m/s²). Use the visualization of a speedometer needle moving at an increasing rate to make this abstract derivative feel physical. It's important to highlight that while we can calculate third or fourth derivatives, acceleration is the highest order usually required to describe the fundamental dynamics of Newtonian systems.

Conclude by challenging the students to sketch an acceleration-time (a-t) graph based on a complex v-t graph featuring linear segments and curves. This exercise reveals whether they can differentiate between constant velocity (zero acceleration), constant acceleration (horizontal line on a-t graph), and changing acceleration (sloped line on a-t graph). This 'graphical translation' skill is vital for the upcoming course project, as it allows them to debug their mechanical simulations by looking at the shapes of their data plots rather than just the raw numbers.

tasks: Given v(t) = 5t^3, find the acceleration function a(t).
Identify the sign of acceleration for a car slowing down while moving in the negative x-direction.
Sketch an acceleration-time graph based on a provided velocity-time graph.

sessions.title: Constant Acceleration Equations
sessions.description: This session derives the 'Big Four' kinematic equations using integral calculus. You will acquire the algebraic tools to solve for unknown motion variables (time, distance, final velocity) when acceleration is uniform, which forms the core of classical problem-solving.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by framing the transition from instantaneous definitions to predictive power. Up until now, calculus has been used to describe a specific moment in time; today, we use integration to bridge those moments together into the 'Big Four' kinematic equations. The central theme of this session is the 'Constant Acceleration Assumption.' I will emphasize that while these equations are the workhorses of classical mechanics, they are only valid when the rate of change of velocity is fixed. This sets the stage for using calculus not just as a tool for slope-finding, but as a method for accumulating change over an interval.

The first derivation starts with the definition of acceleration as the derivative of velocity. I will write $a = dv/dt$ on the board and demonstrate the separation of variables, leading to the integral of $dv$ from $v_0$ to $v$ and the integral of $a \, dt$ from $0$ to $t$. The key takeaway here is that because 'a' is constant, it pulls out of the integral, resulting in the linear relationship $v = v_0 + at$. This reinforces the idea that velocity changes linearly over time when acceleration is steady. I’ll pause here to ask the students what the 'area under the curve' of a constant horizontal line in an acceleration-time graph represents, visually connecting the calculus to the geometry.

Next, we move to the derivation of the displacement equation. We substitute our new expression for velocity into the definition $v = dx/dt$. This leads to the integration of $(v_0 + at) \, dt$. I will explain that the resulting $1/2 at^2$ term is the signature of constant acceleration—the parabolic nature of position. A common misconception I must address here is students forgetting that $v_0$ is also multiplied by 't'. I will describe this as 'the distance the object would have covered anyway' plus 'the additional distance gained by the boost of acceleration.' This conceptual split helps students visualize the two different physical contributors to the total displacement.

To round out the algebraic toolkit, we derive the 'timeless equation' $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x$. I will show this by solving for 't' in the first equation and substituting it into the second, or by using the chain rule identity $a = v(dv/dx)$. This latter method is more elegant and reinforces their calculus foundation. I will present this equation as the 'Energy-Lite' version of kinematics—a way to link speeds and distances directly when the clock isn't the priority. This is particularly useful for the stopping distance problem, which serves as our first major application check.

During the practice segment, I will walk through the car deceleration problem. I’ll challenge students to identify why the acceleration must be negative in their coordinate system if the initial velocity is positive. This reveals whether they truly understand the vector nature of these variables. Finally, we tackle finding the time to reach a specific displacement, which often requires the quadratic formula. I will use this moment to explain the physical meaning of 'two solutions'—one representing the object passing a point on the way up and the other on the way down—ensuring they can distinguish mathematical artifacts from physical reality.

tasks: Derive v = v0 + at using calculus.
Solve for the stopping distance of a car decelerating at 5 m/s^2 from an initial speed of 30 m/s.
Find the time required for an object to reach a certain displacement given initial velocity and constant acceleration.

sessions.title: Free Fall
sessions.description: This session applies constant acceleration kinematics to objects moving under the influence of gravity alone. You will learn to model vertical motion using g = 9.8 m/s^2, providing a concrete real-world application of the 1D motion principles learned so far.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by grounding the abstract kinematic equations derived earlier into the most universal human experience of motion: things falling. The transition from general 'constant acceleration' to 'free fall' is conceptually subtle but physically profound. Start by defining free fall not as 'falling down,' but as motion where the only significant force is gravity. This is a public-lecture style 'aha' moment—explain that an object thrown upward is in free fall from the moment it leaves the hand, despite moving against gravity, because the acceleration vector $g$ is already pulling it back. Use a whiteboard to sketch a simple vertical axis, typically defining 'up' as positive, and establish $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$ as a constant vector pointing downward. Emphasize that the sign of $a$ (usually $-9.8$) is a choice of coordinate system, not an inherent property of the earth, to prevent the common student error of mixing sign conventions mid-problem.

Next, we tackle the symmetry of vertical motion, which is the 'secret weapon' for solving complex problems. Draw a trajectory of a ball thrown upward and caught at the same height. On the whiteboard, illustrate that the time to rise equals the time to fall, and the speed at any given height is identical on the way up and the way down, though the velocity vectors are mirrored. This symmetry allows us to simplify the 'Total Time in Air' problem. Instead of solving a quadratic equation for the whole trip, we can find the time to reach the peak (where $v = 0$) and simply double it. This approach reinforces the concept that acceleration is a constant change in velocity, slicing through the motion with mathematical elegance rather than brute-force calculation.

To address the calculation of maximum height, lead a walkthrough of the 'stopping' condition. The most important idea here is that at the apex of motion, the instantaneous velocity is zero, yet the acceleration remains $-9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$. Many learners mistakenly believe acceleration is zero at the top because the object 'stops.' Correct this by asking: 'If acceleration were zero at the peak, would the ball ever come back down?' This conceptual check prevents future errors in dynamics. Use the equation $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a(y - y_0)$ to solve for height, showing how this specific kinematic tool is optimized for scenarios where time is unknown, further building the student's problem-solving intuition.

Finally, we shift to the 'cliff-drop' scenario to explore impact velocity. Here, the focus is on the accumulation of speed. When calculating the impact velocity of a rock dropped from 50m, emphasize that 'dropped' is a technical term meaning $v_0 = 0$. Use the whiteboard to show how the displacement $\Delta y$ is negative if the cliff top is the origin. This reinforces the discipline of vector signs. Conclude by discussing the limitations of the free-fall model, such as air resistance, to frame this session as a 'idealized' foundation. This prepares students for more complex modeling in their course projects, where they might eventually account for the drag that we are currently ignoring for the sake of mastering the gravitational constant.

tasks: Calculate the maximum height of a ball thrown upward at 15 m/s.
Determine the impact velocity of a rock dropped from a 50m cliff.
Calculate the total time in the air for a projectile launched and caught at the same height.

lectures.title: Motion in Two Dimensions
lectures.description: Expanding kinematics into the plane, dealing with independent horizontal and vertical motions and relative frames of reference.

sessions.title: Position and Velocity Vectors
sessions.description: This session generalizes 1D motion to 2D using vector notation for r(t), v(t), and a(t). You will understand how to treat perpendicular components of motion independently, a critical concept for the course project's modeling of complex 2D paths.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by bridging the gap from the previous 1D kinematics to the reality of a multi-dimensional world. Use the analogy of an ant crawling across a moving piece of paper; the key conceptual leap is that horizontal and vertical motions are not just occurring simultaneously, but are 'orthogonally independent.' Explain that we no longer use a single number to track progress, but a position vector, r(t), which acts as a mathematical 'arrow' pointing from the origin to the object's current coordinates. Emphasize that the beauty of vector notation lies in its ability to package separate x and y differential equations into a single, elegant statement. This transition is vital because it sets the stage for the course project, where modeling complex paths requires tracking components separately before synthesizing them.

Introduce the position vector r(t) = x(t)i + y(t)j on the whiteboard. To make this concrete, use the example of a particle moving along a path where x(t) grows quadratically while y(t) oscillates sinusoidally. This specific example (x=t², y=sin(t)) is crucial because it disrupts the student's expectation of linear or parabolic paths, showing that 2D motion can be arbitrary and complex. Guide the students to see that by treating 'i' and 'j' as independent containers, we can apply the calculus they already know to each dimension without any cross-interference. A common misconception here is that the time variable 't' somehow changes between dimensions; reiterate that time is the universal parameter that 'clocks' both motions simultaneously.

Transition from position to the velocity vector v(t) by applying the derivative operator to the entire r(t) expression. Use the whiteboard to demonstrate that the derivative of a sum of vectors is the sum of their derivatives. When differentiating r(t) = (3t)i + (5t²)j, point out how the 'i' component yields a constant velocity of 3, while the 'j' component yields a time-dependent velocity of 10t. This distinction is the most important idea in this segment: velocity is not just a 'fastness,' but a directional vector. Use this moment to check for understanding: if a particle is moving at a high speed but its velocity vector is purely in the 'i' direction, what is its vertical velocity? This reinforces the concept of component independence.

Finally, address the distinction between the velocity vector and speed (the magnitude of velocity). This is where learners often stumble, as they may confuse the vector v(t) with its scalar counterpart. On the whiteboard, draw a right triangle where the legs are vx and vy and the hypotenuse is the total speed. Use the Pythagorean theorem to derive the magnitude formula. This is the 'synthesis' step: after breaking motion apart to do the calculus, we bring it back together to find the actual physical speed the object would show on a speedometer. This procedure—differentiating components and then finding the magnitude—is a fundamental workflow that students will use throughout the rest of the course, especially when we move into force dynamics and work-energy theorems in later units.

tasks: Write the position vector r(t) for a particle with x(t)=t^2 and y(t)=sin(t).
Find the velocity vector by differentiating r(t) = (3t)i + (5t^2)j.
Calculate the magnitude of velocity (speed) at a specific time t from the velocity vector.

sessions.title: Projectile Motion
sessions.description: This session analyzes objects launched into the air, combining constant horizontal velocity with vertical free fall. You will learn to calculate range, hang time, and peak height, mastering the most iconic application of 2D kinematics.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the common misconception that horizontal and vertical motions are somehow 'mixed' or dependent on one another. Use the whiteboard to illustrate a thought experiment: a bullet fired horizontally and a bullet dropped from the same height simultaneously. The crucial conceptual anchor here is the principle of independence of motion. Explain that gravity is a 'vertical-only' phenomenon, meaning it has no authority over horizontal velocity. This realization transforms a complex 2D problem into two simple, simultaneous 1D problems, which is the foundational strategy for all projectile mechanics.

Transition to the formal setup by drawing a standard Cartesian coordinate system on the whiteboard. Define the initial velocity vector at an angle theta. Break this vector down into its scalar components immediately, showing that v0x = v0 cos(theta) and v0y = v0 sin(theta). It is vital to emphasize that throughout the entire flight (ignoring air resistance), v0x remains a constant, while v0y is subject to a constant downward acceleration of 'g'. This visualization helps students avoid the common error of accidentally applying acceleration to the horizontal component during calculations.

Begin the derivation of the 'Trajectory Equation' by eliminating time from the kinematic equations. Write out the horizontal displacement x(t) and the vertical displacement y(t). Show the algebraic substitution clearly, moving from x/v0x to the quadratic form of y in terms of x. The goal here is to reveal the mathematical 'why' behind the path: because the vertical motion is quadratic in time and the horizontal is linear, the result is a parabola. Point out that the vertex of this parabola represents the maximum height, where the vertical velocity component momentarily hits zero, even though the horizontal velocity is still very much alive.

Introduce the 'Range' formula derivation as a special case where the final displacement y is zero. Guide the students through the trigonometry, highlighting the double-angle identity that appears. This is a perfect moment to discuss optimization: why does 45 degrees provide the maximum range? Use the whiteboard to show how angles equidistant from 45 degrees (like 30 and 60) result in the same range but different hang times and peak heights. This reinforces the idea that while the 'result' (range) might be the same, the 'journey' (trajectory) is defined by the trade-off between vertical flight time and horizontal speed.

Conclude by pivoting to the 'target hitting' problem, which is a reverse-engineering of the kinematics learned. Instead of asking where the ball goes, ask what launch parameters are needed to reach a specific coordinate (x, y). This introduces the reality that for any given target, there might be two possible launch angles (high-arc and low-arc) or none at all if the target is out of range. This prepares learners for the course project, where they must model precise mechanical interactions rather than just observing them, moving them from passive calculation to active system design.

tasks: Calculate the horizontal range of a projectile launched at 20 m/s at a 45-degree angle.
Find the launch angle required to hit a target at a specific (x, y) coordinate.
Show that the path of a projectile is a parabola using the kinematic equations.

sessions.title: Uniform Circular Motion
sessions.description: This session introduces motion at constant speed in a circular path, defining centripetal acceleration. You will learn to distinguish between changes in speed and changes in direction, preparing you for the rotational dynamics covered in Unit 4.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the intuitive but incorrect notion that constant speed implies zero acceleration. To bridge this gap, draw a circular path on the board and place a particle at two nearby points. While the length of the velocity vectors at these points is identical (constant speed), their directions are visibly different. This visualization is the 'concept-first' foundation: acceleration is the rate of change of the velocity vector, not just its magnitude. By subtracting these vectors visually, show that the change in velocity points toward the center, immediately justifying why we call it 'centripetal' (center-seeking) acceleration.

Transition into the geometry of the circle to derive the centripetal acceleration formula without getting bogged down in heavy calculus too early. Use similar triangles—the triangle formed by the position vectors and the triangle formed by the velocity vectors. Explain that as the time interval approaches zero, the ratio of the change in velocity to the velocity magnitude is proportional to the ratio of the arc length to the radius. This reveals the elegant a = v²/r relationship. Emphasize that 'r' is in the denominator because a tighter turn (smaller radius) at the same speed requires a more violent change in direction, an analogy that resonates with anyone who has driven a car through a sharp curve.

Introduce the temporal components of circular motion: period (T) and frequency (f). Instead of just providing formulas, define the period as the 'cost in time' for one full lap. Since the distance of one lap is the circumference (2πr), the speed is simply distance over time (v = 2πr/T). Use this to bridge back to the acceleration formula, showing how a_c can also be expressed in terms of period. A common pitfall for students is confusing frequency and period; clarify this by describing frequency as 'how many laps per second' versus period as 'how many seconds per lap.'

Run a 'mental check' practice by asking the class to predict what happens to the acceleration of a car if it doubles its speed while taking the same turn. Most will intuitively say it doubles, but the v² relationship means it quadruples. Use the specific practice task of a car at 20 m/s on a 50m radius to solidify the math. This reveals whether students are comfortably handling units and the squaring of the velocity. Finish by drawing velocity and acceleration vectors at the 12, 3, 6, and 9 o'clock positions of a circle to demonstrate that while they are always perpendicular, their absolute directions in space are constantly shifting, setting the stage for the non-inertial frames and rotational dynamics they will encounter later in the course.

tasks: Calculate the centripetal acceleration of a car taking a turn of radius 50m at 20 m/s.
Relate the period and frequency of circular motion to the orbital speed.
Identify the direction of the velocity and acceleration vectors at different points on a circle.

sessions.title: Relative Motion
sessions.description: This session explains how to relate observations made in different inertial reference frames using vector addition. You will be able to solve 'boat crossing a river' or 'plane in wind' problems, which are vital for understanding how motion is perceived in multi-body systems.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by challenging the learner’s intuition about 'absolute' motion. In a public lecture style, frame the session with a relatable scenario: if you are walking at 3 mph down the aisle of a train moving at 60 mph, how fast are you going? This immediately introduces the core concept—that velocity is not an intrinsic property of an object, but a relationship between the object and an observer's frame of reference. Use the whiteboard to define the notation for relative velocity, such as V(p/a) for 'velocity of object P relative to frame A,' emphasizing that the order of subscripts is a logical anchor. This prevents the common mistake of adding vectors in the wrong direction.

Transition into the vector addition rule (the Galilean Transformation) by visualizing two different observers: one standing on a dock (the shore) and one on a moving platform (the river). Draw a vector diagram where the velocity of a boat relative to the shore is the vector sum of the boat’s velocity relative to the water and the water’s velocity relative to the shore. The key takeaway here is the 'intermediate frame' logic: to get from Object A to Object C, you must go through Object B. This conceptual bridge allows students to see vector addition as a navigational path rather than just an abstract math problem.

Introduce the 'Boat Crossing a River' problem as the first application. Illustrate a boat aiming straight across a river with a strong current. This is a critical moment to address a frequent misconception: learners often think the current only affects the boat's final position, not its path. By drawing the resultant vector, show that the boat actually moves diagonally relative to the shore. Use this to explain the distinction between 'heading' (where the boat points) and 'course' (the actual path over ground). This reinforces the independence of perpendicular components while showing how they synthesize into a single resultant velocity.

Shift the perspective to an aerial view for the 'Plane in Wind' scenario. This adds a layer of complexity because the goal is often to maintain a specific heading despite a crosswind. Teach the learner to work 'backward' from the desired resultant vector to find the necessary heading. This is a subtle but vital shift in thinking—instead of asking 'where will I end up?', ask 'how must I adjust to end up where I want?'. This practical engineering perspective makes the vector subtraction or addition feel necessary and grounded.

Conclude by generalizing these concepts to the Galilean Transformation in 2D. Briefly mention that while these rules feel like absolute truth, they are technically 'low-speed' approximations that will eventually be challenged by Einstein’s relativity in advanced physics. This 'concept-first' teaser provides a sense of the grander scale of physics. End with a practice task that requires the learner to relate two moving frames—such as two cars moving at different angles—to ensure they can apply the subscript notation and vector addition to any arbitrary system, not just boats and planes.

tasks: Find the velocity of a boat relative to the shore if it heads straight across a river with a current.
Calculate the resultant velocity of an airplane flying north in a crosswind from the east.
Apply the Galilean transformation to relate velocities between two frames moving at constant velocity.

projects.stage_description: Implement a numerical integration loop (Euler method) to calculate the 2D position and velocity of a spacecraft under constant acceleration and initial velocity vectors. This establishes the coordinate system and time-stepping logic for the simulation.
projects.deliverable_increment: A core simulation loop script that outputs time-series data for x and y coordinates and generates a basic trajectory plot.

exams.title: Kinematics Mastery Exam
exams.goal: Verify the student's ability to model motion using vectors and calculus in 1D and 2D environments.
sections: Comprehensive evaluation of vector algebra, 1D motion with constant and variable acceleration, projectile motion, circular motion, and relative velocity.
successCriteria: Correctly set up and solve 1D and 2D kinematic equations.
Demonstrate accurate vector decomposition and addition.
Identify the relationship between position, velocity, and acceleration through derivatives/integrals.
Solve a complex projectile motion problem with non-zero landing height.

units.title: Forces and Newton's Laws
units.description: Transition from how things move to why they move. This unit introduces Newton's three laws of motion and applies them to systems involving friction, tension, and circular paths using free-body diagrams.

lectures.title: Newton's Laws
lectures.description: This lecture establishes the foundational principles of dynamics by defining force and mass through Newton's three laws of motion.

sessions.title: Force and Inertia
sessions.description: This session introduces the qualitative concept of force and Newton's First Law, exploring why objects resist changes in their state of motion. You will learn to identify net forces and understand the physical meaning of inertia as a property of mass. This serves as the critical starting point for dynamics, moving beyond kinematics into the 'why' of motion.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by challenging the Aristotelian intuition that 'motion requires a constant push.' Use a public lecture style to paint a vivid picture of a spacecraft drifting through the vacuum of space at a constant velocity. The goal here is to establish that motion itself is a state, not a process that consumes energy. Explain that Force is not the cause of motion, but rather the cause of the 'change' in motion. This distinction is the bedrock of dynamics; without it, students often revert to the 'impetus' fallacy where they believe an object must have a force in the direction of its travel.

Transition to the formal definition of Newton’s First Law: the Law of Inertia. Define inertia not just as a vocabulary word, but as a quantitative resistance inherent to mass. Use the 'Whiteboard' to visualize a spectrum of mass—from a ping-pong ball to a lead sphere—and ask the learner to imagine flicking both. The core idea is that mass is 'laziness' in a physical sense. Emphasize that 'Uniform Motion' (constant velocity) and 'Rest' are physically equivalent states in the eyes of the First Law. This is the moment to introduce the concept of an Inertial Reference Frame, explaining that our laws of physics only 'behave' correctly when the observer isn't themselves accelerating.

Introduce the 'Net Force' ($̃F_{net}$) as the vector sum of all influences acting on a body. Draw a free-body diagram of a book sitting on a table. Students often struggle with the idea that forces are present even when nothing is moving. Explicitly address the 'Normal Force' and 'Gravity' as a balanced pair, resulting in zero net force. Use this to bridge to the practice task: if the net force is zero, the object is in equilibrium. This doesn't mean no forces exist; it means they are in a perfect tug-of-war. Ask the learner to identify the net force on a car traveling at a steady 60 mph on a straight highway—the common mistake is to assume a forward force exists, but the 'correct' answer in this equilibrium state is zero.

Conclude by applying these concepts to a real-world scenario: a passenger in a braking car. Describe the sensation of being 'thrown' forward. On the whiteboard, illustrate that there is no 'forward force' acting on the passenger; instead, the passenger's inertia is simply trying to maintain their previous state of motion while the car (their reference frame) is being forced to stop by the brakes. This shift in perspective—from feeling like you are being pushed to realizing you are just staying still while the world changes—is the 'Aha!' moment that confirms the learner has grasped the First Law. This sets the stage for the Second Law by defining the baseline of what happens when $̃F_{net}$ equals zero.

tasks: Identify the net force on an object in various equilibrium states.
Explain how inertia affects the motion of a passenger in a braking car using First Law principles.

sessions.title: Newton's Second Law
sessions.description: This session formalizes the relationship between force, mass, and acceleration through the calculus-based vector equation F=ma. You will gain the ability to calculate the acceleration of a particle when subjected to multiple concurrent forces. Mastering this law is essential for all subsequent mechanics, as it provides the primary tool for predicting object trajectories.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by bridging the gap between Newton’s First Law and the reality of changing motion. Start with a conceptual 'What if?' scenario: if the First Law tells us that objects maintain their velocity without a net force, what happens to the physical state of an object the moment a net force is applied? Use the whiteboard to write down 'F ∝ a' (Force is proportional to acceleration) and 'a ∝ 1/m' (Acceleration is inversely proportional to mass). The goal here is to shift from the qualitative 'push' or 'pull' to a quantitative definition. Explain that acceleration isn't just a byproduct; it is the observable response of a mass to an unbalanced force. This sets the stage for F=ma not as a mere formula, but as a definition of force itself.

Transition into the vector nature of the Second Law. It is a common pitfall for students to treat force as a scalar quantity, simply adding magnitudes. On the whiteboard, explicitly write the vector notation ΣF = ma, emphasizing that the summation (Σ) represents the net force. Illustrate this by drawing a single mass subject to two competing forces at odd angles. Show how we must decompose these vectors into Cartesian components (ΣFx = max and ΣFy = may). This is the 'calculus-ready' view of mechanics: we aren't just looking at the total push, but how the components of that push independently dictate the trajectory in 2D or 3D space. This breakdown is vital because it transforms a complex spatial problem into two or three simpler algebraic ones.

Introduce a 'whiteboard practice' moment here. Present a block on a frictionless surface being pulled by a rope at a 30-degree angle. Ask the students to predict which component of the force actually contributes to the horizontal acceleration. The intention is to reveal the common error where students use the full magnitude of the force for horizontal calculation, neglecting the vertical component that might be reducing the normal force. By correcting this early, you reinforce that the direction of acceleration always aligns perfectly with the direction of the net force vector.

Now, connect the dynamics back to the kinematics learned in Unit 1. Present a scenario where a constant force is applied over a specific displacement to change an object's velocity. This is where the 'why' meets the 'how.' Show the logic chain: Force determines Acceleration (F=ma); Acceleration determines the rate of change of Velocity (v² = u² + 2as). By linking these, you demonstrate that Newton's Second Law is the engine that drives the kinematic equations. Explain that in the real world, we rarely know the acceleration beforehand; we calculate it from the forces we can measure, and then we predict the future position of the object. This 'predictive power' is the central theme of classical mechanics.

Conclude by addressing the subtlety of 'mass as inertia' in the context of the equation. Ask why it’s harder to stop a moving truck than a moving bicycle if they have the same acceleration. This allows you to re-center mass (m) as the 'resistance' to the force. On the whiteboard, rearrange the law to a = F/m to show that for a fixed force, an increasing mass leads to a diminishing return in acceleration. This intuitive visualization helps students realize that mass is essentially the 'price' an object pays to change its motion. Wrap up by preparing them for the Third Law, noting that while the Second Law tells us how one mass reacts, we must still investigate where that force actually came from.

tasks: Calculate acceleration for a mass given several force vectors in Cartesian components.
Determine the required force to achieve a specific velocity change over a given displacement.

sessions.title: Newton's Third Law
sessions.description: This session explores the symmetry of interactions, focusing on action-reaction pairs and the distinction between internal and external forces. You will learn to correctly identify force pairs and avoid the common pitfall of thinking they cancel each other out on a single object. This understanding is vital for analyzing multi-body systems and conservation of momentum in later units.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start this session by challenging the common misconception that forces are things an object 'has' or 'possesses.' Shift the focus to the idea that a force is a mutual interaction between two entities. Use the concept-first approach by asking the class to imagine a person pushing against a wall. The person feels a pressure on their hands; this is the physical evidence that while they push the wall, the wall pushes back. This shift from 'force as a property' to 'force as an interaction' is the crucial philosophical leap required to understand Newton's Third Law. Emphasize that in the universe, forces always come in pairs—there is no such thing as an isolated force.

Formally state the Third Law: whenever object A exerts a force on object B, object B simultaneously exerts a force of equal magnitude and opposite direction on object A. On the whiteboard, draw two distinct bodies, A and B, and use clear vector notation (F_AB and F_BA) to represent the interaction. The core idea here is symmetry. Explain that the 'action' and 'reaction' happen at the exact same moment; there is no time delay. It is important to steer students away from the semantic trap that the 'action' causes the 'reaction' in a chronological sense; they are two sides of the same coin.

Address the most significant hurdle in dynamics: the belief that if these forces are equal and opposite, they should always cancel out and nothing should move. To resolve this, use the 'System Boundary' visualization. Draw a single object (e.g., a book) and show only the forces acting *on* it. Then, draw the second object (the table) and show the forces acting *on* it. Explain that forces only cancel if they act on the same object. Newton's Third Law pairs never act on the same object. This is a perfect moment for a practice check: ask students to identify the reaction force to the Earth's gravity pulling down on a book. Most will incorrectly say the normal force from the table. Correct this by tracing the interaction back to the source: if the Earth pulls the book, the book pulls the Earth. The normal force is a separate interaction between the book and the table.

Transition to a more complex, intuitive example: walking. When we walk, we push the ground backward. By the Third Law, the ground pushes us forward. This demonstrates that the force responsible for our motion actually comes from the environment, not our internal muscles alone. Muscles allow us to exert the force on the floor, but it is the floor's reaction that accelerates our mass. This connects the Third Law back to the Second Law (F=ma) and sets the stage for analyzing systems of multiple blocks. 

Conclude by sketching two blocks of different masses in contact, being pushed by an external force. Show the internal contact forces between the blocks. Guide the students to see that while the internal forces (the interaction between block 1 and block 2) are equal and opposite and would cancel if we treated the two blocks as a single system, they are vital for determining the individual acceleration of each block when analyzed separately. This bridge between internal and external forces is what allows physicists to zoom in and out of complex systems, a skill that will be foundational for the upcoming session on Free-Body Diagrams.

tasks: Identify action-reaction force pairs for a book resting on a table and for a person walking.
Sketch the interaction forces between two blocks in contact being pushed by an external force.

sessions.title: Free-Body Diagrams
sessions.description: This session teaches the systematic technique of isolating an object and representing all external forces as vectors. You will acquire a standardized method for setting up physics problems that reduces complex scenarios into solvable algebraic equations. This procedural skill is the single most important tool for success in classical mechanics and engineering analysis.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this capstone session for our study of Newton's Laws, we transition from theoretical understanding to the primary engineering tool of mechanics: the Free-Body Diagram (FBD). We begin by establishing the concept of 'isolation.' I will visualize this by drawing a complex system—perhaps a block on a ramp connected by a string to another weight—and then literally using a dotted line to 'cut' the object of interest away from its environment. The central idea here is that the universe only affects an object through forces that cross this boundary. I want to emphasize that an FBD is not just a sketch; it is a mathematical translation layer that turns a physical scene into a solvable vector equation.

Next, we move to the standard taxonomy of forces. I will demonstrate how to systematically check for interactions: gravitational (always down), normal (always perpendicular to the surface), frictional (always parallel and opposing motion), and tension (always pulling away). A common student error is including 'phantom forces' like the force of the hand that *already* pushed the block or the 'centrifugal force' that doesn't exist in an inertial frame. I will address this by insisting that every vector on the whiteboard must have a specific physical agent—if you can't name the object exerting the force, the force shouldn't be on the diagram.

We then tackle the geometry of the inclined plane, which is the ultimate test of FBD proficiency. I will show how to rotate our coordinate system so that the x-axis aligns with the ramp. This isn't just a trick; it’s a strategic choice to align our axes with the direction of acceleration, which simplifies the math. I’ll demonstrate how the gravitational vector (mg) now needs to be decomposed into components—mg sinθ and mg cosθ. I will use a color-coded approach to show how the angle of the incline relates to the internal triangle of the weight vector, preventing the frequent mistake of swapping sine and cosine functions.

To wrap up, we will perform a 'translation' exercise. Once the FBD is complete, I will show how to write the sum of forces for the X and Y directions independently. This is the moment where physics becomes algebra. I will guide the learners through a practice task: drawing a block being pulled up a rough incline. This specific example forces them to handle gravity, friction, and an external tension vector at an arbitrary angle. By the end of this session, students should see the FBD not as an extra step, but as the essential bridge that ensures the Second Law (F=ma) is applied accurately to every component of motion.

tasks: Draw a complete free-body diagram for a block being pulled up a rough incline at an angle.
Translate a free-body diagram into a set of independent X and Y component equations.

lectures.title: Applying Newton's Laws
lectures.description: This lecture focuses on practical problem-solving using specific force types like tension and friction in multi-object systems.

sessions.title: Weight, Normal Force, and Tension
sessions.description: This session defines common contact and field forces, specifically the gravitational weight, the surface normal force, and the pull of strings or cables. You will learn to calculate these forces in static and dynamic equilibrium scenarios. These represent the most frequent force components you will encounter in any mechanical system design.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by reframing the concept of a 'force' from an abstract push or pull into a specific physical interaction. Because the learner prefers a concept-first, public lecture style, begin with the concept of 'Field vs. Contact.' Explain that Weight (W or Fg) is a field force—a non-touching interaction between the Earth and an object—while the Normal Force and Tension are contact forces, arising only when surfaces touch or strings tighten. The core logic to emphasize here is that while Weight is usually a fixed vector (mg) near the Earth's surface, contact forces are 'reactive'; they only provide as much force as the environment demands, up to a breaking point or a structural limit. This distinction is vital because students often mistakenly treat the Normal Force as always equal to weight, a misconception we must dismantle early by showing how it changes in dynamic systems.

Transition to the 'Normal Force' (Fn) using the visual of a microscopic spring system. Explain that when an object sits on a table, the surface molecules compress like billions of tiny springs; the 'Normal' force is simply the perpendicular push-back from these springs. This is the perfect moment to introduce the elevator thought experiment. Walk through the scenario: when the elevator is stationary, the floor pushes up with exactly 'mg.' However, when the elevator accelerates upward, the floor must not only support your weight but also provide the additional net force required for acceleration (F_net = ma). Contrast this with the feeling of 'lightness' when accelerating downward. The goal is for the learner to see the Normal Force as a scale reading—a dynamic value that reports how hard a surface is pushing to maintain a constraint, rather than a static property of the object.

Introduce Tension (T) as the 'pull-only' counterpart to the Normal Force. Use the concept of an 'ideal string'—massless and unstretchable—to simplify the physics into a pure transmission of force. Visualize a rope as a chain of molecules pulling on each other. The key insight for the learner is that tension is uniform throughout the string and always pulls away from the object it is attached to. To bridge this into 2D problem solving, introduce a hanging sign supported by two cables at different angles. This serves as the first major 'equilibrium' check. Instead of just doing the math, explain the 'why': if one cable is more vertical than the other, it must carry more of the vertical load. Use the whiteboard to resolve these tension vectors into X and Y components, showing that the horizontal components must cancel out for the sign to stay still, while the sum of vertical components must counteract the downward pull of gravity.

Conclude the session by synthesizing these forces into a 'Free Body Diagram' (FBD) workflow. Explain that the FBD is the 'mathematical translator' that turns a physical picture into a solvable equation. The most important takeaway is that once the FBD is drawn, the physics is essentially done, and the rest is just the calculus and algebra they are already comfortable with. Warn against the common error of 'inventing' forces that aren't there—remind them to only look for things touching the object (contact) and gravity (field). This session sets the stage for the next session on Inclined Planes, where we will take these same forces and simply rotate our perspective.

tasks: Calculate the tension in two cables supporting a hanging sign at different angles.
Find the normal force on a person in an elevator accelerating upwards vs downwards.

sessions.title: Inclined Planes
sessions.description: This session applies Newton's laws to objects moving along tilted surfaces, requiring the rotation of coordinate axes. You will learn how to decompose the weight vector into components parallel and perpendicular to the plane. This provides a template for solving a wide class of constraint-based motion problems in physics.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by acknowledging a common psychological hurdle: the tendency to want the world to stay upright. We begin by visualizing a block sitting on a horizontal surface, where gravity points straight down and the normal force points straight up. Then, mentally tilt the surface. The 'aha!' moment for the learner should be the realization that while gravity is stubborn and still points toward the center of the Earth, the surface is now pushing at an angle. This mismatch creates the necessity for a coordinate system shift. Explain that we rotate our axes not because the physics changes, but because it makes the math 'lazy' in the best way possible—by aligning one axis with the direction of motion, we reduce a two-dimensional acceleration problem into a one-dimensional one.

On the whiteboard, draw the inclined plane at an angle theta. Place a mass on it and draw the weight vector (mg) pointing vertically down. This is the crucial juncture where most students fail: the geometry of the triangle. Show how the angle of the incline is identical to the angle between the weight vector and the line perpendicular to the surface. Use a quick geometric proof—complementary angles in a right triangle—to solidify this. This isn't just a math trick; it’s the bridge that allows us to decompose gravity into two distinct roles: one component (mg cos theta) that presses the block into the ramp, and one component (mg sin theta) that tries to win the tug-of-war against friction and pull the block down.

Now, perform the derivation of acceleration for a frictionless block. By summing the forces along the newly defined x-axis (parallel to the slope), we see that the only unbalanced force is mg sin theta. When set equal to 'ma', the mass cancels out. Emphasize the beauty of this result: the acceleration depends only on the tilt of the world and the strength of gravity, not the weight of the object. This is a perfect moment to pause and ask the learners: 'What happens if the angle is 0 degrees? What if it's 90 degrees?' This sanity check helps them see that the sine function correctly predicts zero acceleration on a flat floor and full free-fall (g) when the ramp is vertical.

Transition to the 'stationary' problem to introduce the concept of constraint and external intervention. If the block is to remain still, we must introduce an external force—perhaps a hand pushing or a cable pulling. Challenge the learners to determine if it’s more efficient to push horizontally or parallel to the ramp. This exercise reveals the power of force components: to cancel out that downhill slide of mg sin theta, we need an exactly equal and opposite force. This sets the stage for the next session on friction, as students begin to realize that surfaces themselves often provide this 'stay-still' force automatically, but only up to a point.

Address the common misconception regarding the normal force. Many students reflexively set N = mg out of habit from horizontal problems. Use the whiteboard to show that on a ramp, the surface only needs to support the part of the weight pushing *into* it (mg cos theta). Since cos theta is always less than or equal to 1, the normal force on a ramp is always less than it would be on flat ground. Use the 'elevator' analogy if needed: the ramp is effectively 'falling away' from the vertical gravity vector, lightening the load on the surface. This prepares them for the upcoming friction calculations, where the magnitude of the normal force becomes the gatekeeper for how much grip a surface can provide.

tasks: Derive the acceleration of a frictionless block sliding down a plane inclined at angle theta.
Determine the force required to keep a block stationary on a smooth ramp.

sessions.title: Friction
sessions.description: This session introduces the empirical models for static and kinetic friction and the coefficient of friction. You will learn to predict when an object will start to slide and how friction opposes motion once it begins. This adds a layer of realism to your mechanical models and is crucial for the course project's force analysis.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by challenging the idealized frictionless world we've occupied so far. Explain that friction is not just a nuisance to be ignored, but the very mechanism that allows us to walk, drive, and keep buildings standing. Introduce the concept of friction as a 'reactive' force that arises from microscopic interactions between surfaces. Start the whiteboard by sketching two surfaces magnified at a molecular level, showing 'asperities' or tiny jagged peaks interlocking. This visual helps learners understand that friction isn't just a number in a formula, but a physical resistance to shearing these peaks.

Introduce Static Friction (fs) as a variable force that matches whatever effort is applied to an object, up to a breaking point. Draw a graph of Friction Force vs. Applied Force, showing a 45-degree linear increase. It is crucial to emphasize the inequality fs ≤ μsN. Explain that the coefficient of static friction (μs) represents the 'stickiness' of the interface, while the Normal force (N) represents how hard the surfaces are pressed together. A common misconception for students is treating static friction as a fixed value; clarify that it only takes on the value necessary to prevent motion, and μsN is merely its 'maximum capacity.'

Transition to Kinetic Friction (fk) by showing the sudden 'drop' in the graph once the object starts moving. Explain the physical intuition: once the microscopic peaks are broken or sliding over each other, it's easier to keep them moving than it was to start the motion. Introduce the equation fk = μkN and contrast it with the static inequality. Point out that for almost all materials, μk is less than μs. Use the example of pushing a heavy crate—the hardest part is the first nudge, after which the push feels slightly lighter. This transition is a key 'aha' moment for understanding why we differentiate the two states.

Conduct a practice walkthrough: the 'Maximum Static Friction' problem. Sketch a crate on a floor and provide a specific μs value. Ask the learners to calculate the threshold force required to move it. This exercise serves to solidify the relationship between mass, gravity, the normal force, and the friction threshold. It’s an ideal time to check if they remember that the Normal force isn't always equal to mg (e.g., if someone is pushing down on the crate or it's on a slope), reinforcing the importance of the Free Body Diagram (FBD) developed in previous sessions.

Conclude by solving for acceleration in a sliding system. Set up a scenario where an applied force exceeds the maximum static friction, and the block is now subject to kinetic friction. Guide the learners through the net force equation (F_net = F_applied - fk = ma). This step bridges the gap between static equilibrium and the dynamics of moving systems. Emphasize that while friction opposes the direction of relative motion, it doesn't necessarily 'oppose the applied force'—a subtle but important distinction for later complex systems. This prepares them for the course project where they must account for energy loss due to friction in their mechanical models.

tasks: Calculate the maximum static friction force for a crate on a floor given the coefficient mu_s.
Solve for the acceleration of a sliding block considering kinetic friction effects.

sessions.title: Drag and Terminal Velocity
sessions.description: This session examines velocity-dependent forces, such as air resistance, and the resulting non-constant acceleration. You will learn to set up differential equations for motion in a fluid and calculate terminal velocity. This bridges the gap between idealized vacuum physics and real-world atmospheric motion.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by challenging the simplified 'vacuum world' of physics we've occupied so far. The instructor should start by asking the students to visualize a feather and a hammer dropped simultaneously on the moon versus on Earth. This highlights the concept that in reality, forces are rarely constant; they often depend on the state of the object itself. We introduce 'Drag' as a resistive force exerted by a fluid—like air or water—that opposes motion. The central conceptual shift here is that unlike friction, which we often treat as a constant value once sliding begins, drag is dynamic. It grows as the object speeds up, creating a feedback loop between velocity and net force that demands a more sophisticated mathematical toolset: differential equations.

Transitioning to the whiteboard, the instructor should set up the Free Body Diagram for a falling object. We draw the weight vector pointing down and the drag vector pointing up. The core relationship to establish is F_net = ma = mg - bv (assuming linear drag for simplicity). This is the moment to bridge the gap for students who might be wary of calculus: explain that 'a' is simply the rate of change of velocity (dv/dt). By rewriting the equation as m(dv/dt) = mg - bv, we reveal the 'Differential Equation of Motion.' The key insight is that the acceleration isn't a fixed number anymore; it's a function that changes every millisecond as the object gains speed.

Next, we explore the physical consequence of this relationship: Terminal Velocity. The instructor should lead the students through a thought experiment. If the object starts from rest, v is zero, so drag is zero and acceleration is at its maximum (g). As v increases, the drag force 'eats away' at the net force. Eventually, there must be a point where the upward drag perfectly cancels the downward weight. At this point, the net force is zero. Ask the class: 'If the net force is zero, does the object stop?' This is a critical diagnostic question to catch the common misconception that zero force means zero motion. We must clarify that zero force means zero *acceleration*, leading to a constant, maximum speed. We then algebraically solve for this state by setting dv/dt to zero, deriving V_terminal = mg/b.

To solidify this, the instructor should sketch a qualitative graph of Velocity vs. Time. The curve should start at the origin with a steep slope and asymptotically approach the terminal velocity line. This visualization helps students understand the 'diminishing returns' of gravity in a fluid. We then move to the practice task involving a skydiver. This provides a 'sanity check' for the math—by plugging in realistic values for mass and the drag coefficient, students see how a human body eventually reaches a steady state of about 55 m/s. We conclude by emphasizing that while the calculus allows us to find the exact speed at any moment, the 'Physics' lies in understanding the balance of forces that dictates the limit of that motion.

tasks: Write the differential equation of motion for a falling object with a drag force F = -bv.
Calculate the terminal velocity of a skydiver given mass and drag coefficients.

lectures.title: Circular Dynamics
lectures.description: This lecture applies Newton's Laws to particles moving in curved paths, integrating kinematics from Unit 1 with force analysis.

sessions.title: Centripetal Force
sessions.description: This session identifies 'centripetal force' not as a new type of force, but as the net radial force required for circular motion. You will learn to relate F=ma to centripetal acceleration (v^2/r) and identify which physical forces provide this acceleration. This is essential for understanding how everything from car tires to satellite orbits functions.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the common misconception that 'centripetal force' is an invisible, additional force that magically appears when things turn. Use the 'public lecture' style to frame this not as a new physical entity like gravity or tension, but as a 'job description' or a requirement. Explain that for any object to follow a curved path, the laws of physics demand a net force pointing toward the center of that curve. If that 'job' isn't filled by a real physical force—like a string pulling or tires gripping the road—the object simply won't turn. This shift in perspective is crucial: we are looking for which existing force is acting as the centripetal force, rather than adding a new arrow to our free-body diagram labeled 'Fc'.

Transition into the mathematical derivation of the centripetal acceleration magnitude. Use the whiteboard to briefly recall the direction of the velocity vector at two nearby points on a circle. Show that the change in velocity vector, Δv, points toward the center. Connect this geometric intuition to the formula a = v²/r. Once the acceleration is established, invoke Newton’s Second Law (F=ma) to arrive at F = mv²/r. Emphasize that the 'm' and 'v²/r' represent the motion side of the equation, while the left side must be populated by the sum of physical forces. This prevents the common error of students treating centripetal force as an outward force (centrifugal) or a separate force that balances gravity.

Demonstrate this 'job description' concept with two primary examples. First, the ball on a string: here, the tension in the string is the sole provider of the centripetal acceleration. If the string breaks, the 'job' is vacant, and the ball moves off in a straight line tangent to the circle. Second, use the example of a car turning on a flat road. On the whiteboard, draw the car from a rear view. Students often struggle to identify the force here; clarify that it is static friction between the tires and the road pointing inward. This is a vital moment to explain that without friction (like on ice), the 'job' cannot be filled, and the car fails to turn. 

Introduce a practice moment by asking learners to calculate the tension required for a 2kg mass moving at 5m/s in a 1m radius circle. This task is designed to reveal if they can correctly map the variables to the formula and recognize that the calculated value is specifically the 'Tension' force. Following this, pose a qualitative question: 'If we double the speed, what happens to the required force?' This highlights the squared relationship (v²), showing that small increases in speed require significantly more force to maintain the turn—a core principle for road safety and engineering.

Wrap up the session by previewing the complexity of the next sessions.
