Explain that while we've looked at simple horizontal cases where one force does all the work, real-world scenarios like banked tracks or vertical loops involve multiple forces (like gravity and normal forces) collaborating or competing to fill the 'centripetal job.' This sets the stage for vector decomposition in more advanced dynamics problems.

tasks: Identify the source of centripetal force for a ball whirled on a string and a car turning a corner.
Calculate the required tension to keep a 2kg mass moving at 5m/s in a 1m radius circle.

sessions.title: Banked Curves
sessions.description: This session analyzes how normal forces contribute to centripetal acceleration on inclined tracks. You will learn to calculate the 'ideal' banking angle for a race track where friction is not required for a turn. This demonstrates the sophisticated application of vector decomposition in engineering safety and design.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by posing a fundamental engineering paradox: how can we design a high-speed highway exit or a NASCAR track so that vehicles don't slide off, even if the road becomes perfectly icy? This moves the conversation from the previous session—where we relied on tension or friction—to the geometry of the surface itself. Draw a cross-section of a car on a flat road versus a banked incline. The core conceptual leap here is getting students to see that by tilting the road, the normal force (which usually just supports weight) now has a horizontal component that points toward the center of the turn. This is the 'aha' moment: the road itself is pushing the car around the corner.

On the whiteboard, begin the formal Free Body Diagram (FBD) for a car on a banked curve at an angle θ. This is where most students stumble because they are used to tilting their coordinate axes for problems on inclined planes (setting 'x' parallel to the slope). Intervene here and explain why we must NOT tilt the axes this time. Since the acceleration is purely horizontal (centripetal acceleration towards the center of the circular path), we keep our x-axis horizontal and our y-axis vertical. This choice simplifies the sum of forces in the direction of acceleration. Decompose the normal force into N*cos(θ) acting vertically and N*sin(θ) acting horizontally. This visualization is crucial: it shows that the vertical component must balance the car's weight, while the horizontal component must provide the entire centripetal force required for the turn.

Proceed to the 'Ideal Banking' derivation. Set up the two equilibrium equations: N*cos(θ) = mg and N*sin(θ) = mv²/r. Show the mathematical elegance of dividing these two equations, which cancels the mass 'm' and the normal force 'N', leaving us with tan(θ) = v²/gr. Emphasize the physical implication: the ideal angle depends only on the speed and the radius, not the weight of the vehicle. A heavy truck and a light motorcycle both navigate the same banked curve identically at the design speed. This is a perfect moment for a 'sanity check' exercise: ask students what happens if the speed 'v' increases. They should conclude that since 'tan(θ)' is fixed by the concrete, a higher speed would require a larger force than the normal force can provide alone, necessitating friction to 'help' pull the car inward.

Transition into the more complex scenario where friction is present. This adds a layer of vector decomposition that often overwhelms learners. Draw two cases: the 'Minimum Speed' case (where the car tends to slide down the ramp, so friction points up the slope) and the 'Maximum Speed' case (where the car tends to slide out, so friction points down the slope). Guide the students through adding the friction components to the previous equations. This reveals the 'safety envelope' of a turn—the range of speeds at which a car can safely travel without slipping. This derivation reinforces the idea that centripetal force isn't a single thing, but a 'job description' filled by the sum of components of the normal force and friction.

Conclude by challenging the students to solve for the 'optimal' angle of a real-world highway ramp. Use this to highlight the responsibility of civil engineers. If they calculate an angle for 60mph, but the road gets oily or wet (reducing friction to near zero), the banking is the only thing keeping cars on the road. This connects the abstract calculus and vector math to the tangible reality of public safety, ensuring the concept of 'net radial force' is cemented as a tool for design rather than just a classroom exercise.

tasks: Solve for the optimal banking angle of a highway exit ramp given the design speed and radius.
Analyze the forces on a car on a banked curve with friction present.

sessions.title: Vertical Circles
sessions.description: This session explores non-uniform circular motion where gravity changes the speed of the object along the path. You will learn to calculate the varying normal force or tension at the top and bottom of a loop. This builds the intuition needed to handle energy-based circular problems in the next unit.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by transitioning from the steady state of horizontal motion to the dynamic environment of vertical circles. On a whiteboard, I will draw a classic roller-coaster loop, emphasizing that unlike the previous sessions, gravity now acts along the same axis as the centripetal acceleration at certain points. The central theme of this session is that 'centripetal' is a direction, not a constant value; in a vertical loop, the magnitude of the required net force is fixed by the speed, but the actors—gravity and the normal force—change roles as the object moves from bottom to top.

I will illustrate the 'Bottom' position first. Here, gravity pulls down while the track pushes up. To maintain a circular path, the upward normal force must not only cancel gravity but also provide the necessary $mv^2/r$ acceleration. This leads to the physical sensation of feeling 'heavy' at the bottom of a drop. I’ll guide the learners through the Free Body Diagram (FBD) to show that $N - mg = mv^2/r$. This is a crucial moment to address a common misconception: learners often think gravity provides the centripetal force here, when in fact it is the enemy of the curve, pulling the object away from the center.

Moving to the 'Top' of the loop, the physics shifts dramatically. Now, both gravity and the normal force point toward the center. I will rewrite the equation as $N + mg = mv^2/r$. This leads directly into the concept of 'Critical Speed.' I’ll pose the question: 'What happens if the car goes too slowly?' We’ll mathematically explore the moment the car loses contact with the track, which occurs when the normal force $N$ drops to zero. By setting $N = 0$, we derive $v = \sqrt{gr}$, the minimum speed required to complete the loop. This derivation is the cornerstone of the session, as it connects the abstract vector sum to a life-or-death engineering constraint.

To solidify these concepts, we will walk through a practice problem involving a pendulum at the bottom of its swing. This allows us to swap the 'Normal Force' for 'Tension' and reinforces that the underlying Newton's Second Law application remains identical. I will ask the students to predict whether the string is more likely to snap at the top or the bottom of the swing. Through the FBD analysis, they will see that Tension is at its maximum at the bottom ($T = mg + mv^2/r$), correcting the intuition that speed alone determines the risk of breaking. We conclude by acknowledging that speed in these systems actually changes—a hint at the Law of Conservation of Energy which we will use in the next unit to find exactly how $v$ varies at every point.

tasks: Find the minimum speed at the top of a roller coaster loop for the car to maintain contact.
Calculate the tension in a pendulum string at the bottom of its swing.

sessions.title: Non-Uniform Circular Motion
sessions.description: This session introduces tangential acceleration alongside centripetal acceleration for objects changing speed while turning. You will learn to calculate total acceleration as a vector sum and understand how forces must be applied both radially and tangentially. This completes your mastery of particle dynamics before moving to conservation laws.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by breaking the 'uniformity' constraint that has governed our study of circular motion thus far. In previous sessions, we treated speed as a constant, focusing solely on the change in direction. Today, we bridge the gap between simple rotation and real-world dynamics where objects speed up or slow down while turning. Start by sketching a particle moving along a curved path and prompt the students to consider what happens if the driver of a car hits the gas pedal midway through a curve. This visualization is crucial because it introduces the need for two independent components of acceleration: one to change the direction (radial) and one to change the speed (tangential).

On the whiteboard, derive the total acceleration vector by decomposing it into its radial and tangential components. Explicitly write out the vector sum **a** = **a_r** + **a_t**. The most important concept here is the independence of these two vectors: the radial component (v²/r) is solely responsible for bending the path, while the tangential component (dv/dt) is the linear rate of change of speed. A common misconception is that the tangential acceleration affects the centripetal force; it is vital to clarify that while they occur simultaneously, they represent different physical requirements. Use the example of a car on a track: the friction between the tires and the road must now perform a 'dual role'—part of the friction keeps the car from sliding off the track (radial), while another part pushes the car forward (tangential).

Transition to the dynamics of this motion by applying Newton's Second Law in two dimensions. Draw a free-body diagram for an object in non-uniform circular motion, showing how the net force vector is no longer pointed toward the center of the circle, but is instead angled forward (if speeding up) or backward (if slowing down). This is a 'lightbulb moment' for many students who have been conditioned to think that circular motion always involves a center-seeking net force. Explain that the net force vector points in the same direction as the total acceleration vector. If a particle is slowing down while turning, the net force will point 'behind' the radial line. This logic allows us to solve for the total magnitude of the force using the Pythagorean theorem, which serves as a powerful synthesis of vector calculus and classical dynamics.

To solidify this, lead the class through a practice scenario involving a car increasing its speed at a constant rate while navigating a circular exit ramp. Ask the students to calculate the magnitude of the total acceleration at a specific instant. This exercise reveals whether they can correctly identify which part of the acceleration is constant (the tangential rate) and which part is changing as the speed increases (the radial component). Finally, conclude by summarizing how this session acts as the ultimate bridge: we have moved from the kinematics of how things move in circles to the complex dynamics of why they change speed. This prepares them for Unit 3, where we will see that work and energy provide an even more elegant way to track these speed changes without needing to resolve vector components at every single point on the path.

tasks: Calculate the total acceleration magnitude for a car increasing speed while navigating a circular track.
Determine the net force vector acting on a particle in non-uniform circular motion.

projects.stage_description: Incorporate Newton's Second Law by adding force vectors to the simulation. You will model the spacecraft's mass and the variable force of rocket engines (thrust) to transition from kinematic motion to force-driven dynamics.
projects.deliverable_increment: An updated simulation module that accepts force vectors (thrust) as inputs and calculates resulting acceleration and velocity changes.

exams.title: Dynamics and Newton's Laws Examination
exams.goal: Verify the student's ability to construct free-body diagrams and apply Newton's Laws to solve for the motion of particles in 1D, 2D, and circular paths, including the effects of friction and drag.
sections: Comprehensive evaluation of force analysis including Newton's three laws, friction models, tension, and circular motion dynamics.
successCriteria: Correctly identify all forces acting on a system in a free-body diagram.
Accurately set up and solve coupled F=ma equations for multi-body systems.
Apply centripetal force requirements to circular motion scenarios.
Quantify the effects of static and kinetic friction on object equilibrium and acceleration.

units.title: Energy and Momentum
units.description: Explore the power of conservation laws. You will learn how work, kinetic energy, potential energy, and momentum allow for the solution of complex problems where forces vary over time or space.

lectures.title: Work and Energy
lectures.description: This lecture introduces the scalar approach to mechanics, shifting the focus from vector force analysis to the concepts of work and kinetic energy, providing a powerful framework for solving motion problems without tracking instantaneous acceleration.

sessions.title: Work Done by a Force
sessions.description: This session introduces the formal definition of work as the dot product of force and displacement, including scenarios with varying forces and non-parallel paths. You will learn how to calculate work for constant and variable forces through integration, which is essential for handling realistic physical systems where forces are rarely constant.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by challenging the everyday intuition of 'work.' In common parlance, holding a heavy box stationary feels like hard work, but in physics, this results in zero work. Use this contrast to introduce the concept-first definition: work is the measure of energy transfer that occurs when a force acts through a displacement. This shift from the 'effort' of Unit 2 to the 'outcome' of Unit 3 is vital. Visually, draw a block being pulled by a rope at an angle. This allows you to introduce the dot product not as an abstract math rule, but as a 'component filter'—only the portion of the force pointing in the direction of motion actually contributes to changing the system's state.

Transition to the formal mathematical expression. Explain that if the force is constant, work is the product of the magnitude of force, displacement, and the cosine of the angle between them. However, spend time on the sign of the work. If the angle is acute, work is positive (adding energy); if it's 90 degrees, work is zero (no energy transfer); if it's obtuse, work is negative (removing energy). A common pitfall for learners is forgetting that work is a scalar. Emphasize that while force and displacement are vectors, the result of their interaction is just a number. Use the example of a person carrying a tray horizontally at a constant speed: the vertical normal force does zero work because it is perpendicular to the motion, an insight that simplifies complex force systems significantly.

Move into the calculus-based reality of physics: forces are rarely constant. Introduce the integral definition by visualizing a force-position graph. Explain that the area under the curve represents the total work done. This is the moment to bridge from the algebraic 'F times d' to the integral of 'F(x) dx.' Use the example of a stretching spring or a variable wind resistance to show why we must sum up infinite tiny 'slices' of work. This justifies the prerequisite math (integrals) and shows students that calculus is the natural language for describing physical effort over time and space.

Conclude with a 'zero-work' diagnostic check. Present three scenarios: a moon orbiting the earth (centripetal force), a person pushing against a brick wall that doesn't move, and a puck sliding on a frictionless surface. Ask the class which involves work. This reveals the three ways work fails to happen: zero force, zero displacement, or a 90-degree angle between them. By the end of this session, students should view work not as a feeling of tiredness, but as a precise calculation of how much 'push' actually translated into 'go,' setting the stage for the Work-Energy Theorem in the next session.

tasks: Calculate the work done by a constant force applied at an angle to the displacement.
Evaluate the integral of a position-dependent force to find the total work done.
Identify situations where a force is acting but doing zero work.

sessions.title: Kinetic Energy and the Work-Energy Theorem
sessions.description: This session connects the concept of work to the change in an object's motion, defining kinetic energy and deriving the Work-Energy Theorem from Newton's Second Law. You will be able to solve for the final speed of an object by analyzing the total work done on it, bypassing the need for kinematic equations and time-of-flight calculations.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by framing a fundamental question: if forces represent the 'interaction' (the push or pull), what is the actual 'currency' of motion that is being exchanged? While we previously used Newton’s Second Law to find acceleration and then integrated to find velocity, we are now looking for a more direct shortcut. This session's core purpose is to bridge the gap between the spatial calculation of Work (Force over distance) and the state of the object itself (its energy). Introduce the concept of Kinetic Energy not as an arbitrary formula, but as 'motion in storage.' Use the 'concept-first' approach to explain that any object with mass and velocity possesses a capacity to do work, and the Work-Energy Theorem is simply the accounting ledger that tracks how work done on the object translates into a change in this motion storage.

Transition to the whiteboard to perform a clean, calculus-based derivation that connects the work integral to velocity. Start with the definition of work for a constant force along a line: W = ∫ F dx. Replace F with ma (Newton's Second Law), and then use the chain rule to transform acceleration (dv/dt) into a spatial derivative (v dv/dx). This is a crucial pedagogical moment: by changing the variable of integration from position (x) to velocity (v), we reveal that work is equal to the integral of 'mv dv'. When we evaluate this from an initial velocity to a final velocity, the 1/2mv² term emerges naturally. Emphasize to the students that the '1/2' and the 'square' are not random; they are the direct mathematical consequence of how velocity accumulates over a distance when a force is applied. This removes the 'black box' feel of the kinetic energy formula.

Now, introduce the Work-Energy Theorem formally: Total Work = ΔK. Address a common misconception here: students often forget that 'Work' in this theorem must be the *net* work done by *all* forces. Illustrate this with a scenario of a car braking. If a car is skidding to a stop, the friction does negative work. Ask the students to consider why the work is negative (force is opposite to displacement) and what that means for the kinetic energy. The loss of kinetic energy (slowing down) matches the negative work done by the brakes. This provides an intuitive link: work can either 'charge up' an object’s motion or 'drain' it. Use a quick whiteboard sketch of a car's stopping distance to show that because kinetic energy depends on the square of velocity, doubling your speed doesn't double your stopping distance—it quadruples it. This real-world application reinforces the non-linear nature of the energy-velocity relationship.

Conclude by guiding the students through a 'whiteboard challenge' where multiple forces are present, such as a block being pulled up an incline with friction. Instead of solving for acceleration and using kinematic equations—which is the 'Unit 2' way—show them how to simply sum the work done by the puller, the work done by gravity (negative), and the work done by friction (negative). The sum of these values is immediately equal to the change in (1/2)mv². The goal of this exercise is to prove the 'economy of effort': energy methods allow us to ignore the time it takes for the motion to happen and focus strictly on the start and end states. This 'state-based' thinking is the intellectual leap required for the rest of the course, moving students away from tracking every micro-second of motion toward a more holistic view of physical systems.

tasks: Derive the expression for kinetic energy using the work integral and calculus.
Apply the Work-Energy Theorem to find the stopping distance of a car under constant braking force.
Calculate the final velocity of a particle after several forces have performed work on it.

sessions.title: Potential Energy
sessions.description: This session introduces potential energy as 'stored' energy associated with the configuration of a system, specifically focusing on gravitational and elastic (spring) potential energy. You will learn to define potential energy functions for different forces, providing the necessary tools to model systems that can recover kinetic energy later in their motion.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by reframing our previous discussion of work. In the last session, we saw how work changes an object's state of motion (kinetic energy). Now, we introduce the concept of 'stored' work, or potential energy. Instead of looking at energy as something an object 'has' because it is moving, we shift the perspective to the energy an object possesses due to its position within a system. Use the analogy of a bank account: if kinetic energy is cash being spent on motion, potential energy is the savings account. The transition from the 'Work-Energy Theorem' to 'Potential Energy' is crucial because it allows us to account for work done by internal forces without needing to track every single force vector during the motion.

Begin the whiteboard derivation with Gravitational Potential Energy. Visualize a mass being lifted vertically at a constant speed. Explain that while the total work is zero (since net force is zero), the external agent is doing positive work against gravity. Define the change in potential energy (ΔU) as the negative of the work done by the conservative force (in this case, gravity). This 'negative' sign is often a point of confusion for students; clarify it by explaining that if gravity does negative work (as it does when you lift an object up), the system stores that effort as an increase in potential energy. Write the formula U = mgh on the board, but emphasize that 'h' is relative to an arbitrary reference point. This teaches students that the absolute value of potential energy is less important than the change in energy between two states.

Transition to Elastic Potential Energy using a spring system. Draw a spring at its equilibrium position and then stretched by a distance 'x'. Use Hooke’s Law (F = -kx) to show that the force is not constant, requiring the integral of work we mastered in Session 1. Derive U = 1/2 kx² on the whiteboard. Highlight the quadratic nature of this energy: stretching a spring twice as far doesn't just double the energy; it quadruples it. This provides a perfect opportunity for a quick mental exercise: ask the students to compare the energy needed to stretch a spring from 0 to 1cm versus 1cm to 2cm. This reveals the non-linear relationship and reinforces the importance of the calculus-based approach over simple algebraic multiplication.

Finally, introduce the more abstract but powerful mathematical relationship: Force as the negative gradient of Potential Energy (F = -dU/dx). On the whiteboard, show how taking the derivative of our gravitational and spring energy functions returns the original force formulas. This 'closes the loop' for the learner, demonstrating that potential energy isn't just a separate category of energy, but a mathematical map of the forces acting within a system. Explain that objects naturally 'roll down' the energy hill toward lower potential energy. This conceptual bridge prepares students for the next session on conservative forces and the ultimate goal of Unit 3: the Law of Conservation of Energy.

tasks: Compute the change in gravitational potential energy for an object moved between two heights.
Calculate the potential energy stored in a compressed or stretched spring using Hooke's Law.
Relate the force acting on an object to the negative gradient of its potential energy function.

sessions.title: Conservative and Non-Conservative Forces
sessions.description: This session distinguishes between conservative forces like gravity, where work is path-independent, and non-conservative forces like friction, where energy is dissipated. You will learn how to identify conservative forces using mathematical criteria, which is a critical step before applying conservation laws to ensure the energy 'budget' is accounted for correctly.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by posing a provocative question to the class: 'If you walk up a mountain and then return to the exact same starting point, does your net effort cancel out?' This session bridges the gap between raw calculation and the profound bookkeeping of physics. The core idea is to distinguish between forces that 'save' energy for later (conservative) and forces that 'steal' energy from the system (non-conservative). By framing it as a financial budget, we help students understand that while energy is always conserved in the universe, it isn't always recoverable in a mechanical form.

Begin the whiteboard demonstration by drawing two paths between point A and point B: a straight line and a winding, erratic curve. We will calculate the work done by gravity along both. This visualization is crucial for showing that gravity only cares about the vertical 'drop' or 'rise.' Explain the concept of path independence—the hallmark of a conservative force. This is the moment to introduce the 'closed-loop' test: if you go from A to B and back to A, the net work done by a conservative force is zero. This isn't just a math trick; it's why we can even define 'Potential Energy' in the first place. You cannot have a potential energy function for a force that doesn't pass this test.

Now, contrast this with the 'energy thief': friction. On the same whiteboard, illustrate a block moving in a circle on a rough table. Unlike gravity, friction always opposes the instantaneous direction of motion. This means the work done by friction is always negative and accumulates with every centimeter traveled, regardless of displacement. It is distance-dependent, not displacement-dependent. A common pitfall for students is trying to define 'frictional potential energy.' Use this moment to explain why that's impossible: because the work depends on the 'history' of the path, there is no unique value of 'stored energy' at any given point in space.

Introduce the formal mathematical criterion: the curl of the force field or the gradient relationship. For a force to be conservative, it must be the negative gradient of a scalar potential function. On the whiteboard, show a simple 2D force field, such as F = (y, x), and test it. This connects the abstract calculus the students know to the physical reality of the field. If the path integral around a loop isn't zero, the field is 'curly' or dissipative. This mathematical rigor is what separates a public lecture 'concept' from a true physics mastery, satisfying the learner's request for a concept-first but rigorous style.

Conclude with a 'thought experiment' practice: Have the students imagine a car driving up a hill and back down. Gravity does negative work going up and positive work coming down, netting zero. Air resistance and friction do negative work both ways. Ask them where that 'missing' energy went. This reinforces the idea that non-conservative forces transform mechanical energy into internal/thermal energy, which effectively 'leaks' out of our mechanical model. This transition sets the stage perfectly for the next lecture on the full Law of Conservation of Energy.

tasks: Compare the work done by gravity versus friction over a closed-loop path.
Mathematically verify if a given force field is conservative.
Explain why the work done by friction always depends on the total distance traveled rather than displacement.

lectures.title: Conservation of Energy
lectures.description: This lecture synthesizes work and potential energy into the Principle of Conservation of Mechanical Energy, offering a holistic view of system behavior and introducing power as the rate of energy transfer.

sessions.title: Mechanical Energy Conservation
sessions.description: This session teaches the Principle of Conservation of Mechanical Energy, demonstrating how the sum of kinetic and potential energy remains constant in an isolated system. You will learn to use energy conservation to solve complex motion problems involving hills, loops, and springs, which simplifies the analysis of systems with non-constant accelerations.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the lecture by framing the 'Conservation of Mechanical Energy' not just as a formula, but as a profound accounting principle for the universe. Begin by visualizing a pendulum: as it swings, it seems to 'trade' height for speed and vice versa. Use the whiteboard to define the Total Mechanical Energy (E) as the sum of Kinetic (K) and Potential (U) energy. The core narrative here is that in a closed system without friction, this sum is a 'conserved quantity'—a constant of motion. This is the ultimate shortcut in physics; emphasize that while Newton’s Laws require us to track vectors and forces at every micro-second, energy conservation allows us to 'teleport' from an initial state to a final state by simply looking at the scalar values of speed and position.

Transition into the derivation of the principle from the Work-Energy Theorem. Show that if the work is done only by conservative forces (like gravity or springs), then the work done is equal to the negative change in potential energy. Connect this to the change in kinetic energy to arrive at the equality of the initial and final energy states. This logic chain is vital: students often forget that this 'shortcut' only works when non-conservative forces like friction are absent or do no work. Explicitly warn against the 'friction trap'—explain that the moment heat is generated, our mechanical 'bank account' no longer balances perfectly, which sets the stage for later sessions.

Introduce the first major application: the Roller Coaster. Draw a winding track with various loops and hills. Instead of calculating the normal force and gravity components at every curve, show how we can determine the car's speed at the bottom of a 50-meter drop regardless of the track's specific shape. This reveals the 'path independence' of conservative forces. Pose a challenge: 'If the coaster starts from rest, can it ever reach a hill higher than its starting point?' This leads to the intuition of energy as a 'budget'—you cannot spend more height than you initially 'deposited' into the system.

Shift the focus to elastic systems using a spring-loaded projectile. Draw a horizontal spring compressed by a distance 'x' and then released. This is where many students stumble by trying to use constant acceleration equations (kinematics). Use the whiteboard to demonstrate that because the spring force changes as the spring expands, acceleration is not constant, making kinematics incredibly messy. Energy conservation, however, handles this gracefully by equating the elastic potential energy (1/2 kx²) to the final kinetic energy. This moment should serve as the 'aha!' realization: energy methods are preferred whenever forces vary with position.

Conclude by solving for the equilibrium of a vertical mass-spring system using energy logic. Instead of just balancing forces (mg = kx), show that the point of maximum speed corresponds to the minimum of the potential energy well. This prepares the learner for the next session on energy diagrams. End with a practice prompt: 'A block is dropped onto a vertical spring; calculate the maximum compression.' This exercise is designed to reveal if students remember to include both gravitational and elastic potential energy in their 'account.' It reinforces the idea that we must account for every form of potential energy present in the environment to keep the conservation law valid.

tasks: Solve for the speed of a roller coaster at various points on a track using energy conservation.
Calculate the maximum height reached by a projectile launched from a spring-loaded device.
Determine the equilibrium position of a mass-spring system using energy methods.

sessions.title: Energy Diagrams
sessions.description: This session focuses on the graphical representation of potential energy as a function of position, identifying stable and unstable equilibrium points and turning points of motion. You will gain the ability to predict the qualitative behavior of a particle just by looking at its energy landscape, a skill essential for more advanced physics and engineering modeling.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by framing the potential energy curve $U(x)$ not as a mathematical abstraction, but as a physical 'landscape' or a 'terrain' that a particle must navigate. Use the concept-first approach by drawing a wavy line on the whiteboard and asking the learners to imagine a tiny marble rolling along this track. Explain that the height of the curve represents the stored energy of the system at that specific position. The key intuitive leap here is that the total mechanical energy $E_{mech}$ acts as a 'ceiling' or a horizontal waterline; the particle can never exist where the potential energy curve rises above this line because kinetic energy cannot be negative. This visual constraint immediately transforms a calculus problem into a geometric one, allowing students to see why particles are 'trapped' in certain regions.

Introduce the concept of 'Turning Points' by drawing a horizontal line for total energy that intersects the $U(x)$ curve. Describe these intersection points as the moments where the particle’s velocity hits zero and it must reverse direction, much like a swing reaching its peak height. This is the perfect time to address the common misconception that the particle 'stops' at a turning point—clarify that while the instantaneous velocity is zero, the force is often at its maximum, pushing the particle back into the allowed region. Illustrate the 'Forbidden Regions' where $U(x) > E_{mech}$, emphasizing that classical particles are strictly barred from these zones, which sets the stage for future discussions on quantum tunneling in more advanced physics.

Transition to the analysis of Equilibrium Points by focusing on the 'valleys' and 'peaks' of the graph. Define equilibrium as any point where the slope (the derivative $dU/dx$) is zero, which translates to zero net force. Use the whiteboard to contrast a 'Stable Equilibrium' (the bottom of a valley) with an 'Unstable Equilibrium' (the top of a hill). For the stable case, explain that nudging the particle results in a restoring force that brings it back, creating a 'Potential Well.' For the unstable case, a tiny nudge causes the particle to accelerate away. To deepen the intuition, perform a 'small oscillation' thought experiment: show that near the bottom of any smooth valley, the curve looks like a parabola, meaning every stable system behaves like a simple spring if the displacement is small enough.

Conclude the session by challenging the learners to 'read' a complex energy diagram from left to right. Provide a graph with multiple peaks and valleys of varying heights. Ask them to identify where the particle would move fastest (the deepest valley) and where it would be most 'stuck' (a narrow, deep well). This exercise is designed to reveal if students can successfully map the abstract concept of energy onto the physical reality of motion. End with a bridge to the next session by noting that while the landscape tells us *where* the particle can go, the next logical step is understanding how quickly we can add or remove energy from this landscape—leading into the study of Power.

tasks: Identify stable and unstable equilibrium points on a provided potential energy graph.
Draw the total energy line and determine the allowed and forbidden regions for a particle.
Estimate the period of small oscillations around a local minimum in a potential well.

sessions.title: Power
sessions.description: This session defines power as the instantaneous or average rate at which work is done or energy is transformed. You will learn to relate power to force and velocity, enabling you to calculate the performance requirements for engines, motors, and other mechanical systems found in engineering applications.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by shifting the focus from 'how much' work is done to 'how fast' it is accomplished. While we have spent the previous sessions mastering energy landscapes and conservation, we haven't yet addressed the time dimension. Use the metaphor of two hikers climbing the same mountain: both do the same work against gravity to reach the peak, but the one who finishes in half the time is more 'powerful.' This distinction introduces Power as the time-derivative of work. By framing it as $P = dW/dt$, you link it directly to the calculus-based foundation of the course, ensuring students see power not as a new physical entity, but as a rate of change of an existing one.

Transition into the derivation of the instantaneous power formula by substituting the definition of work ($dW = \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{s}$) into the power equation. Show how $P = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v}$ emerges naturally. This is a critical 'aha!' moment for students because it shifts power from being a post-facto calculation (total work over total time) to a real-time mechanical state. Illustrate this with a car engine analogy: the power output at any given moment depends on how much force the tires apply and how fast the car is already moving. Address the common misconception that a powerful engine always means high speed; explain that it actually means the ability to maintain high force at high speeds, which is why drag forces become the limiting factor in performance.

Demonstrate the practical application of these formulas through the 'Elevator Problem.' Instead of just calculating numbers, walk through the logic of selecting the motor size. If an elevator must lift a specific load at a constant velocity, the motor must counteract gravity. Use this to introduce the Watt ($W$) and the Horsepower ($hp$). It is vital to explain that while the Watt is the standard SI unit (Joules per second), engineering often relies on Horsepower. Providing the conversion factor (1 hp ≈ 746 W) helps bridge the gap between abstract physics and real-world machinery. Ask the students: 'If we want to double the speed of the elevator, what happens to the power requirement?' This forces them to see the linear relationship between power and velocity when force is constant.

Conclude by examining a more dynamic scenario: a vehicle moving against a velocity-dependent drag force, such as air resistance (where $F_{drag} ∑d v^2$). This reveals a non-linear relationship where power required scales with the cube of velocity ($P ∑d v^3$). This 'Power Law' explains why it takes significantly more fuel and engine strength to increase a car's top speed from 100 mph to 120 mph than it does from 40 mph to 60 mph. This discussion prepares students for Unit 5 and real-world engineering constraints by showing that in the presence of dissipative forces, 'more power' is often a requirement just to stay in equilibrium with the environment.

tasks: Calculate the average power required for an elevator to lift a specific load in a given time.
Relate power to force and velocity to find the speed of a car against a constant drag force.
Convert between units of power, such as Watts and Horsepower.

sessions.title: Energy with Friction and External Forces
sessions.description: This session extends the energy principle to non-isolated systems where friction and external work are present, accounting for internal energy changes. You will learn to apply the generalized energy equation to real-world scenarios where mechanical energy is not conserved, bridging the gap between ideal physics models and physical reality.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by acknowledging the 'frictionless vacuum' lie we've lived in for the past few sessions. In reality, mechanical energy is rarely conserved in the sense of remaining constant as $K + U$. The transition from ideal to real-world physics starts here, by expanding our energy accounting system. Instead of viewing friction as a 'loss,' we teach students to view it as a transfer of energy into the internal thermal energy of the system. The central theme is that while 'mechanical energy' ($E_{mech}$) changes, the total energy of the universe remains constant. This is a subtle but vital shift from simple conservation to an energy balance equation.

I will start by drawing a block sliding down a ramp with friction. Rather than jumping to formulas, we'll visualize where the 'missing' energy goes. I'll describe the microscopic interaction—the 'hills and valleys' of the surfaces crashing into each other—explaining that this kinetic energy is being converted into random atomic vibrations, which we perceive as heat. The key equation to introduce here is $W_{ext} = \Delta K + \Delta U + \Delta E_{th}$. I will emphasize that $\Delta E_{th}$ is always positive for friction because friction always opposes motion, doing negative work on the object but increasing the thermal energy of the system. This prevents the common mistake where students subtract friction twice or get confused by the signs in the work-energy theorem.

Next, we tackle the concept of external work. We'll model a scenario where a person pushes a box uphill while friction is present. This allows us to categorize forces into three buckets: conservative (gravity, springs), non-conservative internal (friction), and external (the person pushing). The logic here is that the person adds energy to the system ($W_{ext}$), gravity and height store it ($\Delta U$), motion expresses it ($\Delta K$), and friction 'taxes' it ($\Delta E_{th}$). By framing friction as a 'tax' on every energy transaction, students develop an intuitive sense of efficiency and why perpetual motion is impossible.

We will then walk through a specific calculation: a block sliding down a rough ramp. We'll solve for the final velocity and then compare it to the frictionless case. The delta between these two values represents the energy diverted to thermal energy. I will pause here to ask: 'If the block stops at the bottom, where did all that initial potential energy go?' This prompts the learner to realize it didn't vanish—it's now in the increased temperature of the block and the ramp. This 'detective work' approach to finding energy transforms a dry calculation into a diagnostic tool.

Finally, we will address more complex 'non-isolated' systems, such as a car engine providing a constant force to maintain speed against air drag. This links back to the previous session on power. We'll derive how the chemical energy of the fuel is converted into work to overcome the negative work done by air resistance. This clarifies a major misconception: that 'constant speed' means 'no energy is being used.' By the end of this session, students should see the generalized energy equation not as a new formula to memorize, but as a complete bookkeeping system for every physical interaction they will encounter in engineering or out of the lab.

tasks: Calculate the thermal energy generated by a block sliding down a rough ramp.
Use the generalized energy equation to find the work required to maintain a constant speed against friction.
Model a system where energy is lost to heat and sound during a mechanical process.

lectures.title: Momentum
lectures.description: This lecture introduces momentum and impulse as a vector alternative to energy, focusing on the interactions between objects and the fundamental law of conservation of momentum in collisions.

sessions.title: Momentum and Impulse
sessions.description: This session defines linear momentum and the impulse-momentum theorem, linking the time-integrated force to changes in velocity. You will learn to calculate the average force delivered during short-duration impacts, which is vital for understanding safety engineering and the dynamics of collisions.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the intuition of force. While we've spent Unit 2 looking at Newton's Second Law as F=ma, explain that this is actually a special case of a more fundamental relationship. Introduce the concept of 'Linear Momentum' not just as a formula (p=mv), but as the 'quantity of motion' or the 'persistence of an object’s velocity.' Use the visual of a heavy truck and a light sports car both moving at 30 mph; even though their velocities are identical, the truck's 'quantity of motion' is vastly different. This setup is crucial because it moves the student away from seeing motion purely through acceleration and starts treating mass-in-motion as a combined vector quantity.

Transition into the 'Impulse-Momentum Theorem' by rewriting Newton’s Second Law in its original flux form: Force is the rate of change of momentum (F = dp/dt). On the whiteboard, perform the derivation to show that the integral of force over time equals the change in momentum (J = Δp). This is the 'why' behind the session: we are shifting from looking at forces acting over distances (Work) to forces acting over time (Impulse). It’s vital to emphasize that Impulse is a vector; it has the same direction as the change in velocity. This prevents the common mistake of students treating impulse as a scalar energy-like quantity.

Move into the 'Force-Time Graph' visualization. Draw a bell-shaped curve representing a real-world impact, such as a bat hitting a ball or a car bumper crumpling. Explain that in the real world, force isn't a constant plateau; it spikes and decays. Show that the area under this curve is the Impulse. Introduce the 'Average Force' concept here: a horizontal line that creates a rectangle of equal area to the complex curve. This helps students understand why safety equipment like airbags or padded gloves works—they increase the 'time' component of the impulse to lower the 'force' component for the same change in momentum.

Incorporate a 'Practice Moment' by analyzing a baseball being hit back toward the pitcher. Focus on the vector nature here: if the ball comes in at -40 m/s and leaves at +50 m/s, the change in velocity is 90 m/s, not 10 m/s. This is the most frequent point of failure for students. Use this example to calculate the average force of the bat, assuming a contact time of just a few milliseconds. This reveals the staggering magnitude of forces involved in short-duration collisions, bridging the gap between theoretical physics and engineering reality.

Conclude by framing this session as the foundation for the entire unit. Explain that by mastering the impulse-momentum relationship, we can now solve 'black box' problems where we don't know the exact details of the force during a crash, but we can measure the states before and after. This sets the stage for the next session on conservation, where we will see what happens when these impulsive forces occur between two objects within a closed system.

tasks: Calculate the impulse given to a baseball by a bat using the change in momentum.
Determine the average force exerted during a car crash given the impact time.
Estimate impulse from the area under a force-time graph.

sessions.title: Conservation of Momentum
sessions.description: This session derives the Principle of Conservation of Momentum from Newton's Third Law for isolated systems. You will learn how the total momentum of a system remains constant regardless of internal interactions, providing a shortcut to solving problems involving explosions, recoils, and complex internal forces.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by reframing our view of the universe from a single object to a 'system.' Most students struggle with momentum because they focus too narrowly on one particle at a time. Explain that while Newton's Second Law (F=ma) describes individual objects, we need a broader lens to understand interactions. Introduce the concept of an 'isolated system'—a physical bubble where no external forces penetrate. The core intuition here is that if nothing from the outside pushes the bubble, the 'quantity of motion' inside it must be constant, even if the parts inside are chaotic. Use the metaphor of a closed box of billiard balls: they can crash and bang into each other, but the box as a whole doesn't move unless something outside touches it.

Transition to the formal derivation using Newton’s Third Law. On the whiteboard, draw two particles, 1 and 2, interacting during a collision. Write out that the force of 1 on 2 is equal and opposite to the force of 2 on 1 (F12 = -F21). Show that when we integrate these forces over the time of the collision, the impulses they deliver to each other are exactly equal and opposite. This is the 'aha' moment for the learner: because the change in momentum for object A is the negative of the change for object B, the total change (delta P) for the system is zero. Emphasize that this law is actually more fundamental than Newton's laws themselves, as it holds true even in the quantum and relativistic realms where F=ma begins to fail.

Illustrate the power of this conservation with the classic 'recoil' scenario. Sketch a rifle and a bullet initially at rest. The total momentum is zero. When the trigger is pulled, the explosion is an 'internal force.' Because it's internal, the total momentum must remain zero. This forces the rifle to move backward because the bullet moves forward. A common pitfall for students is forgetting that momentum is a vector; they might try to add the speeds together. Explicitly show that the mass of the rifle times its (negative) velocity must cancel out the mass of the bullet times its (positive) velocity. This provides a 'shortcut'—we don't need to know the complex chemistry of the gunpowder or the friction in the barrel to find the final speeds; we only need the masses.

Move to the 'ice skater' example to solidify the concept of pushing off. This is a crucial practice moment where students calculate the final velocity of two people of different masses. This exercise reveals whether they understand the inverse relationship between mass and velocity change: the lighter person 'wins' more speed from the same interaction. Use this to bridge to the concept of rocket propulsion. Explain that a rocket isn't 'pushing' against the air (a common misconception), but rather it is throwing mass (exhaust gas) out the back at high speed. The rocket moves forward to conserve the system's momentum. Conclude by stressing that conservation of momentum is our most reliable tool for 'black box' problems where the internal details of the force are too messy or fast to measure directly.

tasks: Calculate the recoil velocity of a rifle after firing a bullet.
Solve for the final velocity of two ice skaters pushing off from one another.
Apply momentum conservation to a rocket-propulsion conceptual problem.

sessions.title: Elastic and Inelastic Collisions
sessions.description: This session categorizes collisions into elastic, where kinetic energy is conserved, and inelastic, where it is not, including the special case of 'perfectly inelastic' collisions. You will learn to solve for the post-collision velocities in both cases, which is the cornerstone for analyzing particle interactions and macroscopic impacts.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the common misconception that 'conservation' always applies to everything in a collision. Use a conceptual hook: why do billiard balls bounce apart with a sharp 'clack,' while two lumps of clay stick together with a dull 'thud'? This contrast sets the stage for categorizing collisions not by whether momentum is conserved (which is always true for an isolated system), but by what happens to the system's internal kinetic energy. Explain that while momentum is a consequence of Newton's Third Law, kinetic energy conservation is a high bar that requires no energy to be diverted into heat, sound, or permanent deformation.

Introduce the concept of Inelastic Collisions first, specifically the 'Perfectly Inelastic' case, as it is the most intuitive starting point for the math. Draw two objects of mass m1 and m2 moving toward each other; visualize them merging into a single mass (m1+m2) moving with a common final velocity. The core logic here is that the loss of a degree of freedom (two objects becoming one) simplifies the conservation of momentum equation to a single unknown. This is the perfect moment to pause and ask the learners: 'Where did the missing kinetic energy go?' Use the example of two train cars coupling together to illustrate that the energy is 'spent' on the locking mechanism's friction and the vibration of the cars, even though the total momentum remains perfectly intact.

Transition to Elastic Collisions, where kinetic energy is strictly conserved. This is the most mathematically demanding part of the session because it requires solving a system of two equations: one linear (momentum) and one quadratic (kinetic energy). Instead of getting lost in the algebra immediately, teach the 'Relative Velocity' trick—the idea that in a 1D elastic collision, the speed of approach equals the speed of separation. This provides a much more intuitive grasp of the physics than the raw quadratic formula. Explain that in an elastic world, objects 'see' each other with the same intensity before and after the hit, just in opposite directions.

Deepen the derivation by looking at special cases that build physical intuition. For instance, what happens when a moving ping-pong ball hits a stationary bowling ball? Or when two identical billiard balls collide? Demonstrating that identical masses simply 'swap' velocities is a 'lightbulb' moment for students. It proves that the laws of physics favor symmetry. Address the potential confusion between 'conserved' and 'unchanged'—emphasize that while the total energy of the universe is always conserved, the kinetic energy specifically can be transformed, which is the defining metric for our collision categories.

Conclude with a practice walkthrough that forces a choice. Present a scenario where a car hits a barrier and stops. Ask the students to determine if it was elastic or inelastic based on the damage (deformation) and heat generated. Use this to bridge the gap between abstract particle physics and the macroscopic world of safety engineering. The final exercise should involve calculating the energy 'lost' to the environment in a perfectly inelastic collision, reinforcing that 'lost' doesn't mean 'vanished from existence,' but rather 'moved out of the mechanical system.'

tasks: Solve for the final velocities of two masses after an elastic head-on collision.
Calculate the energy lost in a perfectly inelastic collision between two train cars.
Explain why kinetic energy is not conserved in inelastic collisions despite momentum being conserved.

sessions.title: Collisions in Two Dimensions
sessions.description: This session applies the conservation of momentum to collisions occurring in a plane, treating momentum as a vector quantity with independent components. You will gain the ability to analyze complex grazing collisions, such as those found in billiards or subatomic particle scattering, preparing you for the 2D mechanical modeling required in the course project.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by elevating the previous 1D collision logic into the messy, real world of two dimensions. Begin with a relatable visualization: a game of pool. Explain that while a head-on collision is rare and predictable, a 'grazing' shot is the standard. Use the whiteboard to illustrate that the fundamental beauty of physics here is the principle of independence. Just as we did in kinematics, we treat the X and Y axes as separate stories that must both obey the law of conservation. This conceptual leap is vital because it transforms a complex vector problem into two manageable algebraic ones, allowing us to track objects even when they scatter in wildly different directions.

Transition into the formal setup by drawing a 'before' and 'after' diagram of two particles colliding off-center. Focus heavily on the geometry of the situation, showing how to decompose initial momentum vectors into their horizontal and vertical components using sine and cosine. A common pitfall for students is failing to keep their signs consistent across the entire problem. To prevent this, explicitly define a coordinate system on the board and narrate the process of assigning positive and negative values to momentum based on direction. Emphasize that 'Total Momentum' is not just a sum of magnitudes, but a balance of directional forces.

Introduce a practice scenario where two objects of unequal mass collide and stick together—the 2D perfectly inelastic case. Ask the students to resolve the final velocity vector's magnitude and angle. This exercise is designed to reveal if learners can correctly transition from the component-based math back into a singular physical reality (the final vector). It forces them to use the Pythagorean theorem and inverse tangents, bridging the gap between abstract components and the physical intuition of where the objects actually land.

Move the discussion toward elastic collisions in 2D, such as subatomic scattering. This is where the complexity peaks because we must satisfy both momentum conservation and kinetic energy conservation simultaneously. On the whiteboard, set up the equations to show that we now have three constraints: X-momentum, Y-momentum, and scalar Energy. Address the misconception that energy has 'components'—remind the class that while momentum is a vector that splits into axes, kinetic energy is a scalar that looks at the total speed squared. Use this to demonstrate how we can verify if a collision was truly elastic by comparing the 'before' and 'after' energy states.

Conclude by framing these 2D interactions as the precursor to the course project's orbital or mechanical modeling. Explain that whether it's a satellite docking or particles colliding in a collider, the math is identical. This final segment should leave the student feeling that they have unlocked a universal toolkit for predicting the outcome of any physical interaction in a plane, provided they respect the vector nature of motion.

tasks: Resolve initial and final momentum into X and Y components for a 2D collision.
Find the final direction and speed of two objects after an off-center impact.
Verify energy conservation in a 2D elastic collision example.

projects.stage_description: Calculate the kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy, and work done by the engines at each time step. Create diagnostic plots to ensure mechanical energy is conserved during coasting phases and changes correctly during burns.
projects.deliverable_increment: An energy-monitoring submodule and a graphical plot showing the Energy vs. Time relationship throughout the flight.

exams.title: Energy and Momentum Mastery Exam
exams.goal: Evaluate the student's ability to apply the work-energy theorem and momentum conservation to complex, multi-stage mechanical scenarios.
sections: Comprehensive assessment covering Work, Kinetic/Potential Energy, Conservation of Mechanical Energy, Power, Impulse, and 1D/2D Collisions.
successCriteria: Correctly identify when to use energy conservation versus momentum conservation.
Accurately calculate work for variable forces using integration.
Solve two-dimensional collision problems using vector components.
Interpret potential energy diagrams to predict particle behavior.

units.title: Rotation and Rigid Bodies
units.description: Extend the principles of mechanics to objects with physical size. This unit covers torque, moment of inertia, and the conservation of angular momentum in rigid body systems.

lectures.title: Rotational Kinematics
lectures.description: This lecture translates the familiar concepts of linear motion into the angular domain, providing the mathematical framework for describing rotating systems.

sessions.title: Angular Position, Velocity, and Acceleration
sessions.description: You will learn the formal definitions of angular displacement, velocity, and acceleration, along with their calculus-based relationships. Understanding these variables allows you to describe how an object's orientation changes over time, which is the foundational first step in transitioning from particle mechanics to rigid body dynamics.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the traditional notion of distance. In linear mechanics, we track meters, but in a rotating world, a point near the center of a record player and a point on the edge travel different linear distances while completing the same 'turn.' Introduce the radian not just as a unit, but as the natural ratio of arc length to radius. Explain that by using radians, we strip away the scale of the object to focus on the 'angular' displacement. This is the crucial conceptual leap: moving from tracking a particle's coordinate $(x, y)$ to tracking the orientation $\theta$ of a rigid body as a whole.

Transition to defining angular velocity ($\omega$) by drawing an analogy to linear velocity. Just as $v = dx/dt$, emphasize that $\omega = d\theta/dt$. Use a visual of a spinning ceiling fan to distinguish between average velocity (total turns over time) and instantaneous velocity (how fast it’s whipping around at a specific moment). A common pitfall for students is confusing frequency (Hz) or RPM with angular velocity (rad/s); proactively address this by showing that $2̀π$ radians is the bridge that converts one full 'cycle' into a usable mathematical quantity. The primary goal here is to establish $\omega$ as the rate of change of orientation.

Now, introduce angular acceleration ($̀α$) as the response to a change in spin. If a motor starts from rest and hums to life, its $\omega$ is changing, meaning $̀α = d̀ω/dt$ or the second derivative of position $d^2̀θ/dt^2$. On the whiteboard, set up a functional relationship such as $̀θ(t) = At^3 + Bt$. Ask the students what the 'speed' and 'acceleration' are at $t=2s$. This exercise reveals whether they can apply calculus rules to these new symbols. It’s vital to highlight that if $̀α$ is positive, the object is speeding up its rotation, whereas a negative $̀α$ (angular deceleration) acts as a 'brake' on the spin.

Conclude by tying these three variables together into a coherent hierarchy: position, rate of change, and rate of that rate of change. Remind students that these definitions are the 'grammar' of rotation. Without mastering this language, the dynamics and energy of rotating systems later in the unit will be inaccessible. End with a quick mental check: if a wheel rotates at a constant 10 rad/s, what is its angular acceleration? The realization that constant velocity implies zero acceleration is a simple but essential bridge from their linear motion intuition to this new angular domain.

tasks: Convert angular measurements between degrees, revolutions, and radians.
Calculate average and instantaneous angular velocity for a rotating disk.
Differentiate an angular position function to find angular acceleration.

sessions.title: Constant Angular Acceleration
sessions.description: This session introduces the rotational kinematic equations, which are exact analogs to the constant linear acceleration equations studied in Unit 1. You will be able to predict the future state of a rotating object under constant torque, enabling you to solve complex timing and orientation problems in mechanical systems.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start this session by asking the class to recall the 'Big Three' kinematic equations from Unit 1. Since the learner prefers a concept-first public lecture style, the goal isn't just to hand out formulas, but to demonstrate that physics is a language of patterns. Explain that we aren't learning new physics here; we are simply translating the grammar of straight-line motion into the language of spinning circles. Draw a table on the whiteboard comparing linear displacement (x), velocity (v), and acceleration (a) to their Greek counterparts (θ, ω, α). This visualization is crucial because it lowers the cognitive barrier, helping students realize that if they mastered 1D motion, they have already mastered 70% of rotational kinematics.

Begin the derivation of the angular kinematic equations by assuming a constant angular acceleration. Just as we derived linear equations from a constant 'a', we integrate 'α' with respect to time to arrive at the first equation: ω = ω₀ + αt. Emphasize the physical intuition here—angular velocity changes linearly over time when the 'push' (torque, though we'll formalize that later) is constant. Use the example of a ceiling fan being switched on; it doesn't jump to full speed instantly, but builds up its spin at a steady rate. This is the moment to address a common pitfall: students often forget that these equations only work when alpha is constant. Explicitly state that if a motor's acceleration is changing, we must return to the calculus definitions from Session 1.

Progress to the derivation of the 'timeless' equation, ω² = ω₀² + 2α(Δθ). This is often the most useful tool for engineers because it bypasses the need to measure time, which is frequently the hardest variable to track in mechanical systems. On the whiteboard, show the algebraic substitution of time from the first equation into the displacement equation. This derivation serves a dual purpose: it reinforces the mathematical consistency of our model and provides a powerful 'shortcut' for solving problems where only the start and end states are known. Use the scenario of a car engine's flywheel slowing down to a stop; we know where it started and where it ended, but we might not have a stopwatch running. This equation bridges that gap.

Transition to a practical application by modeling a high-speed motor reaching its operating RPM. This allows for a 'unit-trap' check. Explain that while industry speaks in RPM (revolutions per minute), physics calculates in radians per second. Walk through the conversion process as a necessary hygiene step before any calculation. Ask the learners to solve for the time required to reach a specific speed. This practice task is designed to reveal whether they can identify the 'given' variables versus the 'unknowns'—a fundamental skill in systematic problem solving. If they struggle, guide them back to the 'Big Three' list to see which equation contains their target variable and their known data.

Conclude the session by exploring the total number of rotations a system undergoes during a deceleration phase. This is the synthesis moment. By calculating the total angular displacement and then converting it back to 'rotations' or 'revolutions,' students see the full cycle: from a physical observation, through the mathematical machinery of radians, and back to a tangible physical result. Remind them that while the math uses radians, the 'real world' uses turns. This connection is vital for the upcoming course project, where they will need to model system stability over many cycles of motion.

tasks: Solve for the time required for a motor to reach its operating RPM starting from rest.
Determine the total number of rotations a wheel makes while slowing down to a stop.
Derive the angular version of the 'timeless' kinematic equation.

sessions.title: Linking Linear and Angular Motion
sessions.description: You will explore the bridge between linear and angular quantities, specifically tangential velocity and acceleration. By mastering these connections, you can analyze points on a rotating body in terms of their physical movement through space, a crucial skill for the upcoming project stage involving system stability.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the lecture by challenging the learner's intuition about a record player or a spinning CD. Ask them to visualize two ants sitting on the disk: one near the center and one near the outer edge. While they both complete one full circle in the same amount of time—meaning they share the same angular velocity—their physical experience of 'speed' is vastly different. This session serves as the critical bridge between the abstract world of radians per second and the tangible world of meters per second. We begin by drawing a circular arc on the whiteboard and defining the arc length 's' as the product of the radius 'r' and the angular displacement 'theta'. This is the foundational geometric link; it demonstrates that for a fixed rotation, the further you are from the axis, the more ground you must cover.

Next, perform a live derivation of tangential velocity. By taking the time derivative of the arc length equation (s = rθ) and assuming a rigid body where 'r' is constant, we arrive at v = rω. This is the 'Aha!' moment for many students. I will emphasize that 'v' here is specifically 'tangential'—it is the speed at which a particle would fly off if the string suddenly snapped. A common misconception for learners to avoid is conflating this tangential speed with the angular velocity itself; I will use the 'belt-driven pulley' example to show that while two connected wheels might have different angular speeds, the belt ensures their tangential speeds at the contact points are identical. This is why smaller gears must spin faster to keep up with larger ones.

Transition the discussion from velocity to acceleration, which is where students often get tripped up by the dual nature of circular motion. We must distinguish between tangential acceleration—the rate at which the object is 'speeding up' its spin—and centripetal acceleration, which is the 'center-seeking' force required just to maintain the circular path. On the whiteboard, derive the tangential acceleration (a_t = rα) as the derivative of tangential velocity. Immediately contrast this with the centripetal acceleration formula (a_c = v²/r or ω²r). It is vital to explain that even if a wheel is spinning at a perfectly constant rate (zero angular acceleration), a point on that wheel still experiences centripetal acceleration because its direction is constantly changing. This distinction prevents the common error of assuming 'no change in RPM' means 'no acceleration'.

To solidify these concepts, we will walk through a comparison of different points on a cooling fan blade. We'll calculate the total linear acceleration vector by combining the tangential and centripetal components using the Pythagorean theorem. This practice task reveals whether a student truly understands that these two accelerations are perpendicular to each other. By the end of this session, the learner should see a rotating object not just as a single spinning entity, but as a collection of points, each with a unique linear velocity and acceleration dictated by their distance from the center. This prepares them for the final session on rolling motion, where these linear components must be added to the overall translation of the object.

tasks: Calculate the tangential speed of a point at a specific radius on a rotating platform.
Compare the centripetal and tangential acceleration components of a point on a fan blade.
Determine the linear speed of a belt driven by a pulley of a known diameter.

sessions.title: Rolling Motion
sessions.description: This session examines the unique condition of 'rolling without slipping' as a combination of translation and rotation. You will learn to calculate the velocity of various points on a rolling wheel, providing the necessary insight to model real-world transport and machinery movements in your final project.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by framing 'Rolling Motion' not as a new physical law, but as a beautiful synthesis of everything learned so far: translation and rotation happening simultaneously. I will start the whiteboard by drawing a wheel at rest, then ask the students to imagine the wheel moving in two distinct ways: first, sliding like a block on ice (pure translation), and second, spinning in place like a car stuck in mud (pure rotation). By visually overlaying these two 'ghost' motions on the board, we reveal that rolling is simply the vector sum of both. The primary goal of this opening is to demystify the complexity of rolling by breaking it down into its constituent, simpler parts.

Next, we tackle the 'No-Slip Condition,' which is the most critical conceptual bridge in this session. I will illustrate the contact point where the tire meets the road. Using the vector addition derived in the previous step, I'll demonstrate that for a wheel rolling without slipping, the backward velocity of the rotation must exactly cancel out the forward velocity of the translation at that specific contact point. This leads to the fundamental derivation: v_cm = ωR. It's vital to pause here and emphasize that, for a fleeting instant, the point touching the ground is actually at rest relative to the ground. This is often counter-intuitive for students who assume a moving car means every part of the car is moving at the same speed; I will address this by explaining how this 'static' contact is what allows friction to provide traction rather than heat.

To solidify this, we will perform a 'Vector Map' exercise on the whiteboard. I will draw the wheel again and ask the students to help me plot the velocity vectors for three key locations: the contact point, the center of mass, and the very top of the wheel. We will mathematically prove that while the center moves at 'v', the top of the wheel actually moves at '2v' relative to the ground. This exercise is designed to reveal the non-uniform nature of velocities across a rigid body and prepare them for the more advanced dynamics of Unit 5.

We then transition to the relationship between distance and rotation. If the contact point doesn't slip, then the arc length 's' that the wheel has rotated must be equal to the horizontal distance 'x' the center of mass has traveled. I will derive x = θR and a_cm = αR on the board. This connects back to the kinematics of the previous sessions, showing that if we know how many times a wheel turned, we know exactly how far the vehicle traveled. I will mention that this is exactly how a car's odometer works, but also warn that if the car skids (breaking the no-slip condition), the math fails—bridging the gap between ideal physics and real-world engineering failures.

Finally, we conclude by applying these constraints to a rolling-down-an-incline scenario. Rather than solving for forces yet, we focus on the kinematic description. We will work through a scenario of a cylinder rolling down a ramp to calculate how its center-of-mass velocity is locked to its rotational speed. This prepares the students for the upcoming project work, where they will need to model system stability by understanding that the motion of the whole is constrained by the motion of the parts. I will end by asking them to visualize a bicycle wheel: why do the spokes look blurrier at the top than at the bottom? This leaves them with a physical mystery that confirms our derivation of the '2v' top speed versus the 'zero' bottom speed.

tasks: Sketch the velocity vectors for the top, center, and contact point of a rolling tire.
Relate the center-of-mass velocity to the angular velocity for a cylinder rolling down a ramp.
Solve for the distance traveled by a rolling ball given its angular displacement.

lectures.title: Rotational Dynamics
lectures.description: Move beyond describing motion to analyzing its causes by introducing torque and the rotational equivalent of mass: the moment of inertia.

sessions.title: Torque
sessions.description: You will learn the definition of torque as the 'turning effect' of a force, including the importance of the lever arm and the cross product. This allows you to quantify how forces cause rotation, moving you toward a complete dynamic model of your mechanical system.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by inviting the learners to imagine a heavy door. Ask them why the handle is placed as far from the hinges as possible. This intuitive hook introduces torque not as an abstract vector, but as the 'effectiveness' of a force in causing rotation. The central goal of this session is to bridge the gap between the familiar push-pull of linear dynamics and the pivot-based reality of rotation. We must establish early on that unlike linear force, which only depends on 'how hard' you push, torque depends on 'where' and 'in what direction' that push occurs relative to an axis. 

On the whiteboard, draw a simple wrench gripping a bolt. Illustrate the force being applied at different points. This visualization is crucial for defining the 'lever arm' (or moment arm). Explain the geometry by drawing a line of action for the force and a perpendicular dashed line from the pivot to that line of action. The most common pitfall for students is incorrectly identifying this distance; they often just use the length of the tool regardless of the force's angle. By emphasizing the 'perpendicular' requirement, you teach them to see torque as a product of the force component that actually does the turning work, rather than the total force applied.

Next, formalize the relationship using the cross product: τ = r × F. Since the learner prefers a concept-first public lecture style, explain the cross product as a mathematical tool designed to measure 'perpendicularity.' Draw the vectors r and F starting from the same origin to demonstrate the Right-Hand Rule. Watch for students who struggle with the spatial orientation of the result; emphasize that torque is a vector pointing along the axis of rotation, not in the direction of the motion itself. This is a subtle but vital distinction that separates linear intuition from rotational rigor.

Transition into a brief 'thought experiment' practice involving a see-saw. Ask how two children of different weights can balance each other. This allows you to introduce the concept of 'Net Torque.' If the see-saw is balanced, the clockwise torque must equal the counter-clockwise torque. This isn't just about numbers; it's about the equilibrium of rotational 'influence.' By solving this, students realize that a small force at a large distance can be just as powerful as a large force at a small distance—the fundamental principle of the lever.

Conclude by revisiting the wrench, but this time apply the force at an awkward, non-90-degree angle. Have the students calculate the torque using both the lever arm method and the sine-component method. This dual approach ensures they don't just memorize a formula like Fr sin(theta), but understand the trigonometry behind it.
