End the session by hinting that torque is what will eventually 'drive' the angular acceleration of their project models, setting the stage for the introduction of moment of inertia in the next session.

tasks: Calculate the torque produced by a wrench at various angles of application.
Identify the net torque acting on a balanced see-saw with multiple weights.
Express torque using the vector cross product notation.

sessions.title: Moment of Inertia
sessions.description: This session teaches you how mass distribution affects an object's resistance to rotational change. You will learn to calculate the moment of inertia for discrete particles and continuous bodies, which is essential for understanding why some shapes rotate more easily than others.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by posing a physical puzzle to the audience: why is it harder to start spinning a long, heavy pole than a small handheld dumbbell of the same weight? Introduce the 'Moment of Inertia' (I) not as an abstract formula, but as the rotational twin of mass. In linear motion, mass represents inertia—resistance to changes in velocity. In the rotational world, it is not just the 'stuff' that matters, but where that stuff is located relative to the axis of rotation. Use a whiteboard visual of a point mass at distance 'r' from an axis to establish the fundamental building block: I = mr². Emphasize that the square relationship means doubling the distance has a much more profound effect than doubling the mass, a key intuition for why tightrope walkers use long poles for stability.

Transition to the discrete system by drawing four distinct point masses on the board. Guide the learners through the summation process, showing that the total moment of inertia is simply the arithmetic sum of each individual inertia component. This is a crucial moment to address a common misconception: the axis of rotation is not a fixed physical property of the object itself, but a choice. Redraw the axis in a different location on the same four-mass system to demonstrate how the numerical value of 'I' changes instantly, even though the physical object remains identical. This 'relativity of the axis' is the foundation for all complex dynamics problems that follow.

Introduce the Parallel Axis Theorem as a 'computational shortcut' for when we know the inertia through the center of mass but need to rotate the object around a different point, such as a door swinging on a hinge versus spinning in mid-air. Draw a shape with its center of mass marked and a parallel axis at distance 'd'. Explain the logic: the total inertia is the 'intrinsic' inertia of the shape plus the 'orbital' inertia of the entire object's mass treated as a single point moving at distance 'd'. This separation of 'spinning around oneself' and 'swinging around a point' helps learners mentally decompose complex motions.

Finally, move from discrete dots to continuous solid objects using the language of calculus. For a 'concept-first' lecture, do not get bogged down in the mechanics of integration immediately; instead, explain the 'slicing' logic. Visualize a thin rod as an infinite series of tiny mass elements (dm), each at a different distance (x). Write the integral I = ∫r² dm on the board. Show how we convert 'dm' into a spatial variable using linear density (λ = M/L), allowing us to sum the inertia from one end of the rod to the other. This derivation bridges the gap between simple point-mass intuition and the reality of rigid engineering components, preparing the learner to model real-world mechanical systems where mass is distributed, not concentrated.

tasks: Calculate the moment of inertia for a system of four point masses.
Use the Parallel Axis Theorem to find the moment of inertia about an off-center axis.
Set up the integral to find the moment of inertia of a thin rod.

sessions.title: Newton's Second Law for Rotation
sessions.description: You will combine torque and moment of inertia to form the rotational version of F=ma. This enables you to calculate the angular acceleration of any rigid body, providing the core predictive power needed for the rotational modeling stage of your course project.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by bridging the gap between the familiar and the new. Remind the learners that in Unit 2, they mastered the idea that a net force causes a change in linear motion (acceleration). Now, draw a direct visual parallel on the board: if mass is resistance to linear motion and force is the pusher, and if we've already defined torque as the rotational pusher and moment of inertia as the resistance, it stands to reason there must be a 'bridge' equation. Write $\sum F = ma$ on the left and $\sum \tau = I\alpha$ on the right. This concept-first approach emphasizes that physics is symmetrical; we aren't learning new laws, but rather translating a universal truth into a different coordinate system.

Transition into a formal but intuitive derivation. Instead of just stating the formula, imagine a single point mass $m$ at a distance $r$ from an axis. Apply a tangential force $F_t$ to it. From Newton's second law, $F_t = m a_t$. Now, 'rotationalize' this by multiplying both sides by $r$. The left side becomes $F_t r$ (Torque), and since $a_t = r \alpha$, the right side becomes $m(r\alpha)r = mr^2 \alpha$. Point out that $mr^2$ is exactly what we defined as the moment of inertia for a point mass. This 'aha!' moment is crucial—it proves that $\tau = I\alpha$ isn't just an analogy, but a direct consequence of $F=ma$ applied to rotating bodies. Address the common pitfall here: students often forget that $\alpha$ must be in radians per second squared for this relationship to hold, as the geometric derivation relies on the arc length relationship.

Now, introduce the 'Pulley with Mass' problem to ground the theory in a practical scenario. Draw a mass hanging from a string wrapped around a disk-shaped pulley. In early physics, we treated pulleys as massless, but now we must account for the torque required to spin the pulley itself. Guide the class through a dual-analysis: write the linear $F=ma$ for the falling block and the rotational $\tau = I\alpha$ for the pulley. The key logic to highlight is the constraint of motion—the linear acceleration of the block is tied to the angular acceleration of the pulley ($a = r\alpha$). Solving these simultaneously reveals that the system accelerates slower than it would with a massless pulley. This demonstration is vital because it shows that 'missing' energy or force in real-world machines is often hidden in the inertia of the rotating components.

Conclude the session with a whiteboard walkthrough of a falling yo-yo or a rolling object. This pushes the logic further by showing a system that is both translating and rotating simultaneously. Focus the instruction on the choice of the pivot point—usually the center of mass—and how the tension provides the torque. Warn learners about the sign convention: it is easy to mix up the direction of torque and acceleration. Advise them to always define the direction of expected motion as positive for both linear and rotational vectors to maintain consistency. The practice task of calculating a flywheel's deceleration due to friction serves as a diagnostic check: if a student can find the negative $\alpha$ given a frictional torque, they have successfully synthesized the relationship between torque, inertia, and the resulting change in motion.

tasks: Find the angular acceleration of a flywheel subject to a constant frictional torque.
Analyze a pulley system where the pulley's mass is not negligible.
Solve for the linear acceleration of a falling yo-yo using torque equations.

sessions.title: Rotational Kinetic Energy
sessions.description: This session introduces the energy stored in a rotating object. You will learn to calculate total kinetic energy as a sum of translational and rotational components, which is a vital part of the energy-budgeting requirements for your final mechanical system report.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by bridging the gap between what students already know about linear kinetic energy and the reality of a rotating rigid body. The central challenge to pose is: if every atom in a spinning wheel is moving at a different speed, how can we talk about a single 'energy' for the whole object? On the whiteboard, we draw a generic rigid object and isolate a single tiny mass element, m_i. We visualize its circular path and express its individual kinetic energy as (1/2)m_i(v_i)^2. By substituting the tangential velocity (v = ωr), we show that the kinetic energy becomes (1/2)m_i(r_i^2)(ω^2). This transition is crucial because it reveals that while the linear velocity v varies across the object, the angular velocity ω is the common thread that unites every particle in the rotation.

Next, we perform the summation across all particles to derive the formula K_rot = (1/2)Iω^2. The focus here isn't just on the math, but on the profound symmetry between (1/2)mv^2 and (1/2)Iω^2. We emphasize that the moment of inertia, I, is not just a mathematical convenience but the literal distributor of energy in a rotating system. A common misconception for students is treating rotational and translational energy as two 'different kinds' of energy; we must clarify that rotational energy is simply the collective linear kinetic energy of all internal parts, organized through rotation. Using a spinning space station as a conceptual example helps learners visualize how massive amounts of energy can be stored without the center of mass moving an inch.

We then transition to the concept of 'Total Mechanical Energy' for objects that both translate and rotate, like a rolling ball or a falling yo-yo. We visualize this as a two-channel energy budget: K_total = (1/2)Mv_cm^2 + (1/2)I_cmω^2. The critical insight here is that for 'rolling without slipping,' the two channels are locked together by the constraint v = ωR. On the whiteboard, we should diagram a hoop, a disk, and a sphere at the top of an incline. Instead of just giving them the answer, we ask them to predict which reaches the bottom first. This exercise reveals the 'tax' that rotation places on the system: because some potential energy must be diverted into spinning the object, there is less left over for forward speed. The more inertia an object has far from its center (like a hoop), the higher the 'rotation tax' and the slower it translates.

Finally, we apply the Work-Energy Theorem to rotational systems. We explain that just as Work = Force × distance, Rotational Work = Torque × angular displacement. This is best illustrated by a 'whiteboard' derivation of a grinding stone slowing down due to friction. We show how the negative work done by a frictional torque directly subtracts from the rotational kinetic energy. This prepares students for their final project by showing them how to account for energy losses in mechanical linkages. We conclude by revisiting the rolling objects on the incline, solving for the final velocity of a hoop specifically to prove that the mass and radius actually cancel out, leaving only the shape (the distribution of mass) as the deciding factor in its kinetic behavior.

tasks: Calculate the rotational kinetic energy of a spinning space station.
Apply the work-energy theorem to a rotating grindstone.
Determine the final speed of a hoop rolling down an incline using energy conservation.

lectures.title: Angular Momentum and Equilibrium
lectures.description: This lecture covers the conservation laws for rotation and the conditions required for an object to remain perfectly still.

sessions.title: Angular Momentum
sessions.description: You will define angular momentum for both particles and rigid bodies. This concept is the rotational counterpart to linear momentum and is essential for analyzing systems where the axis of rotation or the mass distribution changes over time.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by acknowledging the intellectual bridge we are crossing. In Unit 3, we mastered linear momentum (p = mv) as a measure of translational 'oomph.' Now, in a public lecture style that prioritizes conceptual clarity over rote memorization, we introduce Angular Momentum (L) as the rotational analog. The core idea to impress upon the learner is that just as mass resists change in linear motion, moment of inertia resists change in rotational motion. We start with the simplest case: a single particle moving in space. The teacher should draw a point mass 'm' moving with velocity 'v' and define a position vector 'r' from an arbitrary origin. The definition L = r × p is not just a cross-product; it is a measure of how much the particle is 'circling' that specific point. It is vital to emphasize that angular momentum depends entirely on the chosen origin—a concept that often confuses students who think of momentum as an intrinsic property of the object alone.

Moving from the abstract particle to the concrete rigid body, we transition to the formula L = Iω. This is the 'moment of inertia times angular velocity' relationship that mirrors p = mv. To make this intuitive, we should describe a spinning wheel: every atom in that wheel has its own individual 'r × p', and when we sum them all up, the geometry of the object (its moment of inertia, I) becomes the scaling factor. The important distinction to make here is that while 'p' is always in the direction of 'v', 'L' is only in the direction of 'ω' for symmetric objects rotating about their principal axes. This is a perfect moment to introduce a mental visualization: a spinning top. Its L-vector points along the axis of rotation, representing the 'persistence' of its spin.

Next, we derive the fundamental relationship between torque and angular momentum: τ = dL/dt. This is the rotational version of Newton's Second Law (F = dp/dt). The logic chain here is critical: if a force causes a change in linear motion, a torque must cause a change in rotational motion. By showing that the rate of change of angular momentum is exactly equal to the applied net torque, we provide the learner with a powerful predictive tool. If they know how L is changing, they know the forces at play; if they know the torques, they can predict the future state of the rotation. This provides the 'why' behind why objects speed up or slow down their spins.

To solidify these concepts, we turn to the first practice task: a planet in an elliptical orbit. At the perihelion (closest point), the radius 'r' is small and velocity 'v' is high. By calculating L = mrv (since r and v are perpendicular here), the learner sees that the product remains constant even as the individual variables change. This prepares them for the next session on conservation. We then pivot to the solid sphere calculation to demonstrate how to use the moment of inertia (I = 2/5 MR²) within the L = Iω framework. A common pitfall for learners is forgetting to check if the axis of rotation passes through the center of mass; the teacher should explicitly prompt the learner to verify the axis before selecting the formula for 'I'.

Finally, the session concludes by tying the cross-product definition back to the derivative of L. We ask the learner: if a torque is applied for a short time, what happens to the L-vector? This 'impulse-like' thinking helps bridge the gap between static definitions and dynamic change. We emphasize that angular momentum is not just a number, but a vector in space, and its direction tells us about the stability and orientation of the system. This sets the stage for the next session, where we will see what happens when the external torque is zero and the system is left to its own devices.

tasks: Calculate the angular momentum of a planet in an elliptical orbit at perihelion.
Determine the angular momentum of a rotating solid sphere.
Relate torque to the rate of change of angular momentum.

sessions.title: Conservation of Angular Momentum
sessions.description: You will explore the principle that angular momentum remains constant in the absence of external torques. This explains phenomena from figure skating spins to pulsar rotation and is a key tool for solving complex interaction problems without needing to know every internal force.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by drawing an immediate parallel to the conservation of linear momentum. Just as an object’s velocity remains constant unless acted upon by a net force, a rotating object’s angular momentum remains constant unless a net external torque is applied. This is the 'Symmetry of Nature' argument: if space is isotropic (the same in all directions), angular momentum must be conserved. This theoretical foundation is crucial because it allows us to analyze systems with changing shapes or internal movements—like a collapsing star or a spinning athlete—without needing to calculate the messy internal forces involved.

To make this concrete, let's sketch the classic 'Ice Skater' or 'Diver' scenario. On the board, draw a simplified figure with arms extended, then the same figure with arms tucked in. The core insight here is the inverse relationship between the moment of inertia (I) and the angular velocity (ω). As the mass moves closer to the axis of rotation, 'I' decreases, forcing 'ω' to increase to keep the product 'L' constant. This is a perfect moment to address the common misconception that the skater is 'speeding up' because they are doing work; while they are indeed doing work to pull their arms in, the 'why' of the speed increase is governed by the conservation law itself. If the learner asks about energy, acknowledge that kinetic energy actually increases, but momentum is the invariant quantity we track to find the new speed.

Next, we transition to a more complex 'Impulse' problem: a moving particle colliding with and sticking to a pivoted rod. This is a critical bridge for the learner. We draw the particle approaching the rod and ask the pivotal question: 'Is linear momentum conserved?' The answer is no, because the pivot exerts an external force. However, by choosing the pivot as our origin, the torque from that pivot force is zero, meaning angular momentum *is* conserved. This teaches the learner to strategically choose their reference point to make the math vanish. We show how to calculate the initial angular momentum of a point mass moving in a straight line (L = rmv sinθ), which often feels counter-intuitive to students who think 'angular' only applies to circles.

Finally, we explore the 'Gyroscopic Stability' of a bicycle wheel. Instead of heavy math, we use vector diagrams on the board to show the angular momentum vector pointing along the axle. We explain that to change the direction of this large vector, a significant torque is required. This 'resistance to change' in the orientation of the spin axis is why a moving bike stays upright while a stationary one tips. This connects the abstract conservation law to a lived experience, reinforcing that conservation isn't just about speed, but about the stubbornness of a system's rotational state. We conclude by setting a challenge task: if a diver doubles their rotational speed, by what factor must their moment of inertia have changed? This ensures the learner can flip the logic from observation back to the mathematical ratio.

tasks: Predict the final angular velocity of a spinning diver who pulls their limbs in.
Analyze the collision between a moving particle and a pivoted rod.
Explain why a bicycle is more stable when the wheels are spinning rapidly.

sessions.title: Static Equilibrium
sessions.description: You will learn the two necessary conditions for an object to be at rest: the sum of forces and the sum of torques must both be zero. This is the foundation of structural engineering and will allow you to ensure the physical stability of your modeled system in the project.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by framing the concept of 'nothing happening' as a precise physical state. In previous units, we focused on why things move; today, we focus on why they don't. The primary goal is to transition from the intuitive sense of balance to the rigorous application of the two conditions for static equilibrium. Start the 'whiteboard' session by drawing a large, irregular object. We establish that for this object to remain stationary, it isn't enough for the center of mass to be still; the object must also refuse to rotate. This leads us to our first formal definitions: the vector sum of all external forces must be zero, and the vector sum of all external torques must be zero. Emphasize that while the force condition prevents translational acceleration, the torque condition is what prevents the 'spins.'

A critical conceptual pivot is the 'Arbitrary Pivot Rule.' This is often where students struggle—they look for a physical hinge where none exists. I will demonstrate on the whiteboard that if an object is truly in equilibrium, the net torque is zero about *any* point we choose. This is our mathematical superpower. We can strategically place our imaginary pivot at the location of an unknown force (like a complex hinge force or a friction point) to make its lever arm zero, effectively 'vanishing' that unknown from our equation. This isn't just a trick; it's the fundamental logic of structural analysis. I'll illustrate this by setting up a beam problem, showing how choosing the wall-contact point as the pivot simplifies the math compared to choosing the beam's center.

Moving into the first practice task involving the cable and beam, we will address the 'Hidden Angles' misconception. Students frequently apply the force of gravity or tension directly without considering the sine of the angle between the force vector and the position vector. On the board, I will draw the beam and decompose the tension into its components, showing that only the component perpendicular to the beam provides the torque needed to counteract gravity. This moment reveals whether students truly understand the 'r sin theta' relationship or are just memorizing formulas. It's a perfect time to ask: 'If we move the cable closer to the wall, does the tension increase or decrease?' This forces an intuitive grasp of lever arms before they crunch the numbers.

The ladder problem introduces the complexity of friction and multi-contact points. We will visualize the ladder as a system of four forces: gravity at the center, the normal force from the ground, the normal force from the wall, and the friction at the base. The 'aha!' moment here is realizing that the wall's push and the ground's friction must exactly balance each other horizontally. We will walk through the logic of why a ladder might slip if the angle is too shallow, connecting the torque caused by the person climbing it to the required friction force at the bottom. This prevents the mistake of treating friction as a fixed value rather than a reactive force.

Finally, we will bridge equilibrium with the concept of the Center of Gravity. I will show that for most terrestrial problems, the center of gravity and center of mass are the same, but we treat gravity as a single force acting at this point to simplify our torque equations. We conclude by analyzing a composite object—like a heavy sign hanging from a non-uniform pole—to demonstrate how to find the 'balance point.' This serves as a transition to the next session, proving that understanding where the mass 'lives' is the final piece of the stability puzzle. By the end of this session, the learner should see a bridge or a skyscraper not as a static pile of materials, but as a dynamic dance of opposing forces and torques perfectly canceled out.

tasks: Calculate the tension in a cable supporting a heavy horizontal beam.
Find the forces exerted by the ground on a ladder leaning against a wall.
Determine the center of gravity of a composite object using equilibrium principles.

sessions.title: Center of Mass
sessions.description: This session formally defines the center of mass and explains why it serves as the balance point for translational dynamics. Understanding the center of mass is critical for predicting the stability and trajectory of any non-point-like mechanical system.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by challenging the assumption that we can always treat objects as simple dots in space. While we've spent the previous lectures simplifying cars to points and planets to particles, the reality of 'Angular Momentum and Equilibrium' requires us to acknowledge that real objects have size and shape. I start by tossing an irregularly shaped object—like a wrench or a hammer—into the air with a spin. While the ends of the tool follow chaotic, loopy paths, there is one magical point that traces a perfect, smooth parabola. This 'average' position of the system's mass is what we define as the Center of Mass (CM). In a public lecture style, I frame this as the 'representative point' of the object: the place where gravity seems to pull on the whole thing and the point through which Newton’s second law still holds true even if the object is tumbling.

To move from intuition to formalization, I transition to the whiteboard to define the Center of Mass mathematically. I introduce it as a weighted average. For a system of discrete particles, the position of the CM is the sum of each mass multiplied by its position, all divided by the total mass. I illustrate this using a 2D plane with three particles of different masses at various coordinates. The key pedagogical move here is to show that the CM will always be 'pulled' toward the heaviest particle. I purposely place a very large mass near the origin and small masses far away to show how the CM remains close to the 'heavy' part. This prevents the common misconception that the CM must be at the geometric center; learners must see it as a balance of mass, not just distance.

Next, we tackle continuous objects, specifically the 'L-shaped' plate. This is a classic conceptual hurdle because the Center of Mass for this shape actually lies in the empty space outside the physical material. I draw the L-shape and show the technique of 'decomposition'—breaking the complex shape into two simpler rectangles. We find the CM of each rectangle (which is easy by symmetry) and then treat those two points as 'virtual particles.' By calculating the CM between these two points, we prove that the balance point can exist where there is no mass at all. This is a crucial realization for the course project; if students are modeling a satellite or a pendulum with an irregular arm, they must understand that the pivot point or the center of gravity might not be a physical part of the frame.

I conclude the session by connecting this back to translational dynamics. I present a scenario where a system of objects (like two astronauts pushing off each other) is moving through space. Even as the individual parts fly apart or change their relative positions, if there is no external net force, the Center of Mass continues to move at a constant velocity—or remains at rest. This reinforces the 'Conservation' theme of the unit. I end with a thought experiment: if you are standing on a frictionless ice pond and try to walk forward, your feet move back while your torso moves forward, but your Center of Mass stays exactly where it was. This demonstrates that internal forces can never change the motion of the system’s center, providing a powerful tool for predicting the behavior of complex mechanical systems without needing to track every internal collision.

tasks: Find the center of mass for a system of three particles in a 2D plane.
Locate the center of mass of a uniform L-shaped plate.
Describe how the center of mass of a system moves when no external forces are present.

projects.stage_description: Model the spacecraft as a rigid body and implement torque-based rotations. You will calculate the moment of inertia and simulate the angular acceleration needed to reorient the craft for a 'retro-burn' to prepare for lunar arrival.
projects.deliverable_increment: A rotation simulation component that tracks the angular orientation (theta) and angular velocity of the spacecraft.

exams.title: Rotation and Rigid Bodies Unit Exam
exams.goal: Evaluate the learner's ability to apply rotational kinematics, torque, moment of inertia, and angular momentum conservation to rigid body systems.
sections: This comprehensive exam covers the translation of linear quantities to angular ones, the calculation of rotational dynamics using Newton's Second Law for rotation, the application of energy and momentum conservation in rotating systems, and the principles of static equilibrium.
successCriteria: Correctly solve rotational kinematic problems for displacement, velocity, and time.
Calculate moments of inertia for basic shapes and composite systems.
Apply the conservation of angular momentum to systems with changing mass distribution.
Successfully solve static equilibrium problems involving both force and torque balance.

units.title: Oscillations and Gravitation
units.description: Synthesize the course through the study of periodic motion and universal gravitation. The unit concludes with an introduction to fluid mechanics and wave behavior as coupled oscillators.

lectures.title: Simple Harmonic Motion
lectures.description: This lecture introduces the physics of repetitive motion, exploring how restoring forces lead to predictable periodic behavior in systems like springs and pendulums.

sessions.title: Springs and Hooke's Law
sessions.description: This session introduces the linear restoring force provided by ideal springs and the mathematical definition of Hooke's Law. You will learn to calculate the force exerted by a spring and the potential energy stored within it, establishing the foundational physics required to understand any oscillating system.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by grounding the abstract concept of a 'restoring force' in a tangible physical experience. Imagine holding a ruler at the edge of a desk, pulling it down, and feeling it fight back to return to its original level. This internal resistance is the heart of periodic motion. In this 'whiteboard' session, we begin by visualizing an 'ideal' spring—one that is massless and frictionless—at its natural length, which we label as the equilibrium position (x = 0). The most critical takeaway here is that the force a spring exerts is always 'backward-looking'; it wants to return to zero. This is why we write Hooke's Law as F = -kx. The negative sign is not just a mathematical detail; it is the directional signature of a restoring force, indicating that the force vector is always opposite to the displacement vector. 

Transition into the physical meaning of the spring constant 'k'. Visualize two different springs on the board: one from a ballpoint pen and one from a heavy-duty truck suspension. By comparing them, you demonstrate that 'k' represents the 'stiffness' or the 'personality' of the spring. A common pitfall for students is treating 'k' as a variable rather than a property of the material. Use this moment to perform a quick mental check: if a 10N force stretches a spring by 2cm, what force is needed for 4cm? This reinforces the linear nature of the relationship before moving into more complex dynamics. Emphasize that Hooke's Law is a 'linear approximation'—real springs eventually deform permanently or break, but for the 'Small-Angle Approximation' and standard SHM we will study later, this linearity is our fundamental assumption.

Now, shift the focus from force to energy. We must explain that because the force of a spring changes as it is stretched (unlike the constant force of gravity near Earth's surface), we cannot simply multiply Force times Distance to find the work done. This is a perfect opportunity to use the whiteboard to plot Force vs. Displacement. The area under the linear slope (a triangle) reveals the formula for Elastic Potential Energy: U = 1/2 kx². Explain that this energy is 'stored' in the lattice of the material itself. It is vital to emphasize that the energy scales with the square of the displacement; doubling the stretch doesn't double the energy—it quadruples it. This quadratic relationship explains why high-amplitude oscillations require significantly more energy input.

Wrap up the session by connecting these two concepts through a practice walkthrough. Ask the students to imagine a mass hanging vertically. Here, the restoring force of the spring is fighting the constant force of gravity. By setting the magnitude of the spring force equal to the weight (mg), they can solve for 'k'. This reveals how we calibrate instruments in the real world. Then, transition to calculating the stored energy at that specific equilibrium point. This prepares them for the next session, where we will stop looking at static snapshots and start looking at the 'dance' of energy as it sloshes back and forth between potential and kinetic states in a full oscillation.

tasks: Calculate the spring constant for a mass-spring system given displacement and force.
Determine the elastic potential energy stored in a compressed spring.

sessions.title: Simple Harmonic Motion
sessions.description: This session derives the differential equation for simple harmonic motion and explores its sinusoidal solutions involving amplitude, frequency, and phase. You will be able to describe the position, velocity, and acceleration of an oscillator as functions of time, which is essential for predicting the state of any periodic mechanical system.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by bridging the gap between the intuitive push-and-pull of a spring and the formal language of calculus. Start with the 'Force Balance' equation: by equating Newton's Second Law (F=ma) with Hooke's Law (F=-kx), we arrive at a second-order differential equation. The most critical point here is to emphasize the negative sign; it reveals that acceleration is always proportional to displacement but in the opposite direction. This is the mathematical signature of Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM). Instead of solving the differential equation formally, we will 'guess' the solution by asking what kind of mathematical function returns to itself (with a negative sign) after being differentiated twice. This naturally leads us to the sine and cosine functions, making the transition from force to wave-like motion feel like a discovery rather than a definition.

Next, we break down the anatomy of the position function, x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ). Each variable must be personified: Amplitude (A) is the 'reach,' Angular Frequency (ω) is the 'pace,' and the Phase Constant (φ) is the 'starting line.' A common student pitfall is confusing ω with linear frequency; clarify that ω represents how many radians of the 'circle of motion' are swept per second, linking the oscillating spring to a point moving around a circle. This visualization helps demystify why we use trigonometric functions for linear back-and-forth movement. We will then derive the relationship where ω equals the square root of k/m, showing that stiffness increases the pace while mass slows it down due to inertia.

Moving into kinematics, we derive velocity and acceleration by taking time derivatives of our position function. This is a crucial moment for 'whiteboard' visualization: draw the graphs of position, velocity, and acceleration stacked vertically. Highlight that when position is at a maximum (the turning point), velocity is zero, and acceleration is at its negative maximum. This reveals the logic of the system—the moment the object stops, the restoring force is strongest, trying to pull it back. We will specifically focus on finding V-max (ωA) and A-max (ω²A). It is essential to explain that these maximums occur at different points in the cycle, preventing the misconception that all maximum values happen simultaneously.

To solidify these concepts, we transition to a practice moment centered on 'state-setting.' We will challenge the learner to write the equation of motion for a system that doesn't start at the equilibrium or the maximum stretch, but somewhere in between. This requires solving for the phase constant (φ). This exercise is designed to reveal if the learner understands that SHM is a continuous cycle and that our 'time zero' is just an arbitrary snapshot. We conclude by calculating the maximum velocity for a specific spring-mass setup, forcing the learner to synthesize their understanding of the spring constant, mass, and amplitude into a single predictive value, confirming they can now navigate from the physical properties of hardware to the temporal behavior of the system.

tasks: Solve for the maximum velocity of an object in SHM given its amplitude and frequency.
Write the equation of motion for a mass-spring system starting from a non-zero phase.

sessions.title: Energy in Oscillation
sessions.description: This session examines the continuous transformation between kinetic and potential energy in an ideal oscillator. You will learn how to use energy conservation to solve for system variables at any point in the cycle, providing you with a powerful tool to analyze motion without needing to solve complex differential equations directly.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by reframing the mass-spring system not as a series of force vectors, but as an elegant 'energy exchange engine.' The central goal is to demonstrate that while position and velocity are constantly changing, the total mechanical energy remains a bedrock constant. Begin the whiteboard derivation by writing the expression for total energy E as the sum of Kinetic Energy (1/2 mv²) and Elastic Potential Energy (1/2 kx²). The key conceptual leap for students is realizing that at the 'turning points' (amplitudes), the velocity is zero, meaning all energy is potential. Conversely, at the equilibrium position, the potential energy is zero, meaning all energy is kinetic. This symmetry is the most important idea because it allows us to bypass the time-dependent sine and cosine functions entirely when we only care about the state of the system at a specific location.

Deepen the intuition by sketching a 'potential energy well'—a parabolic graph of U = 1/2 kx². Draw a horizontal line representing the constant total energy E. Show how the gap between this line and the parabola represents the kinetic energy available at any position x. This visualization helps prevent the common misconception that energy is somehow 'lost' during the transition; instead, it's just shifting between two distinct buckets. Address a frequent point of confusion: students often think energy is maximized at the amplitudes because the force is strongest there. Use the whiteboard to explicitly contrast 'maximum force' with 'maximum kinetic energy' to clarify that the center of the motion is actually where the system is 'most alive' in terms of speed.

Introduce a practice moment by asking the class to calculate the velocity of the mass when it is exactly halfway to its maximum displacement (x = A/2). Many students will instinctively guess that the velocity is also half of its maximum value. This is a crucial 'trap' to set. By working through the energy equation (1/2 kA² = 1/2 mv² + 1/2 k(A/2)²), you will reveal that the velocity is actually √3/2 of the maximum. This algebraic result is powerful because it proves that the energy distribution is non-linear; the system spends more of its 'energy budget' on speed near the center than it does near the edges. This realization transforms their understanding from a linear intuition to a quadratic one, which is essential for all future studies in oscillations.

Conclude by generalizing the power of the energy method. Explain that while Newton’s Second Law gives us the 'how' (the path), energy conservation gives us the 'limits' (the speed and range). This approach is often more robust in real-world physics because it holds true even if the internal details of the motion are complex, provided the system is conservative. Prepare the transition to the next session by hinting that in real systems, 'damping' acts like a leak in this energy container, slowly lowering the horizontal total energy line until the motion ceases. This session equips students with a shortcut—a scalar tool that simplifies the vector-heavy burden of kinematics.

tasks: Calculate the total mechanical energy of an oscillating system.
Find the velocity of a mass when it is at half its maximum displacement using energy methods.

sessions.title: Pendulums and Damping
sessions.description: This session applies SHM principles to simple and physical pendulums under the small-angle approximation and introduces the effects of dissipative forces. You will understand how gravity acts as a restoring force and how real-world friction leads to damped oscillations, bridging the gap between ideal models and practical engineering scenarios.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by transitioning from the horizontal world of springs to the vertical world of the simple pendulum. The central conceptual shift here is identifying gravity, rather than a spring, as the source of the restoring force. Draw a simple pendulum of length L and mass m at an angle θ. It is crucial to resolve the gravitational force into components—specifically highlighting that the radial component is balanced by tension, while the tangential component, -mg sin(θ), is the lone driver of motion. This provides a direct physical link back to our previous SHM models: we have a force that wants to bring the system back to equilibrium (θ = 0).

To bridge the gap between complex trigonometry and simple harmonic motion, we introduce the 'Small-Angle Approximation.' Visually compare the arc of a circle with a straight horizontal line on the whiteboard to show that for small θ, sin(θ) is approximately θ in radians. This simplification is the 'key' that unlocks the linear differential equation we solved earlier. Without it, the pendulum's motion is chaotic and non-linear; with it, it becomes a predictable harmonic oscillator. We then derive the period T = 2π√(L/g), emphasizing that the mass m cancels out—a counter-intuitive point that often surprises students. This is a perfect moment to ask: 'If I double the mass of a grandfather clock’s bob, does it tick slower?' The realization that it doesn't reinforces the idea that gravity scales with mass, cancelling the effect on acceleration.

Next, we expand the scope to the 'Physical Pendulum.' Instead of a point mass on a string, imagine an arbitrary shape—like a baseball bat or a ruler—pivoting around a point. We use the concept of Torque (τ = r x F) and the Moment of Inertia (I) from Unit 4 to show that any rigid body can undergo SHM if displaced slightly. The logic chain here is: Gravity acts at the Center of Mass, creating a torque proportional to the displacement. By mapping this to the SHM template, we find the period depends on the distribution of mass. This allows us to explain why a short ruler swings faster than a long one, grounding the abstract math in tactile, everyday experience.

Finally, we address the 'Elephant in the Room': air resistance and friction. We transition from ideal SHM to Damped Oscillations by adding a velocity-dependent drag force (-bv) to our equation of motion. Rather than getting bogged down in the complex calculus of the general solution, we focus on the energy profile and the 'Envelope' of the motion. Sketch a sine wave whose peaks gradually decay over time. Use this visual to explain the three regimes of damping: Underdamped (it swings but dies out), Overdamped (it's like moving through honey—it barely returns to center), and Critically Damped (the fastest return to equilibrium without overshooting). This distinction is vital for engineering; students should understand that we want a car's suspension to be critically damped for comfort, whereas we want a musical instrument's string to be underdamped to produce sound.

tasks: Derive the period of a simple pendulum using the small-angle approximation.
Qualitatively describe the difference between underdamped and overdamped motion.

lectures.title: Gravitation
lectures.description: This lecture explores the universal law that governs the motion of planets and stars, applying Newton's laws to astronomical scales.

sessions.title: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
sessions.description: This session presents the inverse-square law that describes the gravitational attraction between two point masses. You will learn how to calculate the gravitational force between any two objects in the universe, which serves as the starting point for understanding orbital mechanics and celestial dynamics.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the common misconception that gravity is something that only happens 'down' towards the Earth. Use the narrative of Newton's 'Great Synthesis'—the realization that the same force causing an apple to fall is the force keeping the Moon in its orbit. The core objective here is to shift the learner's perspective from gravity as a local terrestrial phenomenon to a universal, mutual interaction between all matter. Explain that every particle with mass in the universe attracts every other particle, effectively weaving a web of invisible 'tethers' across space.

Introduce the formula for the Universal Law of Gravitation: F = G(m1m2/r²). Instead of just writing the variables, build the intuition behind the inverse-square law. Ask the learners to visualize a light source: as you move away, the light spreads out over an area that grows with the square of the distance, meaning the intensity drops off sharply. Explain that gravity 'spreads' its influence in the same geometric way. This is a critical moment to emphasize that 'r' is the distance between the *centers* of the masses, not their surfaces; a common pitfall for students when calculating forces between large celestial bodies like the Earth and Moon.

Transition into the significance of the Universal Gravitational Constant (G). Describe G not just as a number, but as the 'strength' of the cosmic fabric. Contrast G with 'g' (acceleration due to gravity) to prevent the chronic confusion between the two. Highlight that G is incredibly small (10^-11), which explains why we don't feel a gravitational pull toward our laptop or the person sitting next to us, even though the law says it exists. It takes a truly massive object—like a planet—for this force to become noticeable to our senses.

Conduct a guided calculation of the force between the Earth and the Moon. This serves as a practical check to handle large scientific notation and to see the 'magnitude' of celestial mechanics. Once the number is found, immediately pivot to a conceptual thought experiment: what happens if we move the Moon? If the distance triples, does the force become a third? Lead the learners to realize it drops to one-ninth. This 'scaling thinking' is more important for mastery than the arithmetic itself, as it forces them to internalize the quadratic relationship between distance and force. Conclude by reinforcing that this force is a vector and follows Newton's Third Law: the Moon pulls on the Earth just as hard as the Earth pulls on the Moon, a fact that often feels counter-intuitive but is foundational for understanding tides and orbital stability.

tasks: Calculate the gravitational force between the Earth and the Moon.
Explain how the force changes if the distance between two masses is tripled.

sessions.title: Gravitational Field and Weight
sessions.description: This session defines the gravitational field as a vector field and explains the variation of 'g' with altitude and planet mass. You will be able to distinguish between mass and weight in different environments, allowing you to model forces on objects in non-terrestrial or high-altitude settings.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by pivoting from the 'action-at-a-distance' concept of the Universal Law of Gravitation to the more sophisticated concept of the gravitational field. Rather than just seeing gravity as a tug-of-war between two masses, we frame the Earth (or any mass) as an object that modifies the space around it. The field $g$ is introduced as a vector that exists at every point in space, even if no second mass is present to experience it. This shift is crucial for a 'concept-first' lecture because it prepares students for electromagnetism and general relativity later. I’ll start by sketching a planet and drawing invisible lines of influence pointing toward the center, representing the acceleration field. This visual helps dismantle the common misconception that gravity is a 'thing' objects have, rather than a property of the space surrounding them.

Next, we derive the mathematical expression for the gravitational field strength $g = GM/r^2$. The key teaching beat here is demonstrating that this field strength is exactly equivalent to the acceleration an object would experience in free fall. By setting the gravitational force equal to $ma$, we show that the mass of the smaller object cancels out. This explains the 'Galilean miracle'—why a hammer and a feather fall at the same rate in a vacuum. I will emphasize that while mass is an intrinsic property (how much 'stuff' there is), weight is merely the local measurement of the gravitational field's interaction with that mass. This distinction is vital for solving problems in non-terrestrial environments, as it prevents students from accidentally treating $9.81$ m/s² as a universal constant.

To apply this logic, we move to the Martian surface. Calculating $g$ for Mars requires students to synthesize two different variables: the planet's smaller mass (which decreases gravity) and its smaller radius (which increases gravity because you are closer to the center). This provides a perfect opportunity to discuss the 'Inverse Square Law' in a physical context. We then transition to the altitude problem: at what height does gravity drop by half? Students often make the mistake of thinking the altitude must be twice the Earth's radius. By working through the algebra on the whiteboard, we reveal that the total distance $r$ must increase by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$, which means the altitude is actually much lower than they expect. This numerical surprise reinforces the non-linear nature of gravity.

Finally, we address the 'weightlessness' myth often seen in public science discourse. We explain that astronauts on the International Space Station still experience about 90% of Earth's gravity; they aren't 'away' from the field, they are simply in a state of continuous free fall within it. We wrap up by visualizing how the gravitational field vector shrinks as we move infinitely far away, but theoretically never reaches zero. This session bridges the gap between 'ground-level' physics and the orbital mechanics of the next session, ensuring students see $g$ not as a number to memorize, but as a dynamic variable determined by the geometry of the universe.

tasks: Calculate the acceleration due to gravity on the surface of Mars.
Determine the altitude at which the gravitational field is half of its surface value.

sessions.title: Orbits and Kepler's Laws
sessions.description: This session connects centripetal force with gravitation to explain circular and elliptical orbits, culminating in Kepler's three laws of planetary motion. You will learn to calculate orbital periods and speeds, which is a critical skill for the final stage of your course project involving satellite or orbital modeling.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the lecture by framing the concept of an 'orbit' not as a mystical floating state, but as a perpetual state of freefall. Use the classic 'Newton’s Cannon' thought experiment to bridge the gap between terrestrial and celestial physics. Explain that if a projectile is launched fast enough, the curvature of the Earth falls away beneath it at the same rate the projectile falls toward it. This visualization is crucial because it demystifies the idea that planets or satellites are 'beyond gravity'; rather, they are moving so fast laterally that they never hit the ground. This sets the stage for the fundamental derivation: equating the gravitational force with the required centripetal force for circular motion.

On the whiteboard, derive the orbital velocity formula by setting GMm/r² equal to mv²/r. Highlight the profound result: the mass of the orbiting object (m) cancels out. This is a critical moment to stop and ask the class why a feather and a space station would orbit at the same speed at the same altitude. This reinforces the equivalence principle introduced earlier in the course. Once the velocity formula v = sqrt(GM/r) is established, use it to calculate the speed of a satellite in Low Earth Orbit (LEO). This practical application grounds the theory, showing that 'falling' around the Earth requires a staggering speed of roughly 7.8 km/s. Address the common misconception that satellites are weightless because there is no gravity; explain instead that they are in a state of 'weightlessness' because they and their surroundings are all falling together.

Transition from circular motion to Kepler’s Laws by introducing Johannes Kepler’s empirical observations. Start with the First Law (Ellipses) and explain that while we often approximate orbits as circles for simplicity, nature prefers ellipses with the sun at one focus. Use the Second Law (Equal Areas) to explain orbital conservation of angular momentum without getting bogged down in complex calculus yet—simply show that a planet must move faster when it is closer to the sun (perihelion) to 'sweep' the same area as it does when it is farther away (aphelion). This builds intuition for the varying speeds observed in planetary orbits.

Dedicate the final segment to the derivation of Kepler’s Third Law (The Law of Harmonies). By substituting v = 2πr/T into the orbital velocity equation, show how T² is proportional to r³. This is the 'aha!' moment of the session, where the empirical observation made by Kepler in the 1600s is shown to be a direct mathematical consequence of Newton’s Law of Gravitation. This derivation is essential for the course project, as it allows students to predict the orbital period of any body if they know its distance from the center of mass. Conclude by having students calculate the period of a LEO satellite, showing it takes roughly 90 minutes to circle the Earth, which provides a tangible sense of scale for space operations.

tasks: Derive Kepler's Third Law for a circular orbit.
Calculate the speed of a satellite in a Low Earth Orbit (LEO).

sessions.title: Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Velocity
sessions.description: This session introduces the general form of gravitational potential energy and the concept of escape velocity using energy conservation. You will learn the minimum energy required for an object to break free from a planet's gravity, enabling you to analyze the energetics of space exploration and rocket launches.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin by challenging the conventional notion of potential energy that students learned in earlier units. Up until now, we have used the formula mgh, assuming a constant gravitational field. Ask the students: what happens when we move thousands of miles away from Earth? The core idea here is that 'g' is not a constant, and therefore, our energy model must evolve. Introduce the concept of the gravitational potential energy of a two-body system as a negative value, specifically U = -GmM/r. It is crucial to explain the 'negative' sign not just as a mathematical result of integration, but as a physical representation of being in a 'gravity well'—an object must gain energy just to get back to zero, which we define as infinitely far away. This shift in reference point from the ground to infinity is the most difficult conceptual leap for students, so visualize it on the whiteboard as a deep well where the surface of the planet is at the bottom.

Transition into the formal derivation by integrating the universal law of gravitation force from a starting radius to infinity. During this whiteboard derivation, emphasize that work is the integral of force over distance. Show how the negative sign naturally emerges and explain that as the distance 'r' increases, the potential energy becomes 'less negative' (i.e., it increases), which aligns with our intuition that lifting something higher increases its energy. Address the common misconception that negative energy means the object has 'less than nothing'; clarify that it represents the 'binding energy' of the system. If the total energy is negative, the object is trapped; if it is zero or positive, the object can escape. This logic chain perfectly sets the stage for the concept of escape velocity.

Now, introduce the scenario of a rocket launch to define escape velocity. Start with the principle of Conservation of Mechanical Energy. Set the initial state as the object on the planet's surface with some kinetic energy and its initial potential energy, and the final state as the object at 'infinity' with zero velocity and zero potential energy. This is the 'minimum' condition for escape. Solve for the velocity 'v' to derive the escape velocity formula. Point out a fascinating detail: the mass of the escaping object cancels out. Whether it is a pebble or a space station, the speed required to leave Earth is the same. This highlights that escape velocity is a property of the planet's mass and radius, not the projectile itself. This is a great moment to pause and ask students why we don't just launch rockets at this speed immediately—leading to a brief discussion on atmospheric drag and multi-stage propulsion to ground the theory in reality.

Move into the practice phase by having students calculate the escape velocity for Earth and then compare it to a planet with different characteristics, like Mars or Jupiter. This exercise reveals how much 'harder' it is to leave a massive, dense planet. For the second practice task, guide them through calculating the energy required to move a satellite from a low-altitude orbit to a high-altitude one. This requires them to sum both kinetic and potential energy for both states. They will discover that while potential energy increases as they go higher, the kinetic energy required for a stable orbit actually decreases. This counter-intuitive result—that you must slow down to stay in a higher orbit—is the 'aha!' moment of the session, reinforcing the deep connection between energy and orbital mechanics.

tasks: Calculate the escape velocity from the surface of the Earth.
Determine the change in potential energy when moving a satellite from one orbit to another.

lectures.title: Extending Mechanics
lectures.description: This lecture expands the principles of mechanics to continuous media, introducing the fundamentals of fluid behavior and wave propagation.

sessions.title: Pressure and Fluids at Rest
sessions.description: This session explores the concept of pressure in static fluids and how it varies with depth. You will learn to apply Pascal’s principle to hydraulic systems, providing a transition from particle mechanics to the mechanics of deformable substances.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by framing the transition from 'hard' particle mechanics to the 'soft' world of fluids. Explain that until now, we have treated objects as rigid points or bodies where forces act on specific locations. In a fluid, we can't easily point to one spot; instead, we talk about 'pressure.' Use the intuitive analogy of walking on snow with boots versus snowshoes. This establishes pressure not just as a formula, but as the distribution of force over an area (P = F/A). Emphasize that in a static fluid, this pressure acts in all directions equally—a concept that often confuses students who think gravity only makes pressure push 'down.' Visualize a tiny cube of water suspended in a tank; if the pressure wasn't equal on all sides, that water cube would accelerate.

Next, derive the relationship between pressure and depth, often called the hydrostatic equation. Start by considering a vertical column of fluid with density 'rho'. The key insight here is that the pressure at the bottom must support the entire weight of the fluid column above it plus the atmospheric pressure pushing down on the surface. Show the step-by-step logic: Mass equals density times volume, and weight is mass times gravity. By dividing this weight by the cross-sectional area, the 'area' term cancels out, revealing that pressure depends only on depth (h), not the shape of the container. This 'hydrostatic paradox'—that a thin tube of water can exert the same pressure as a wide lake at the same depth—is the crucial takeaway. Use this to explain why your ears pop at the bottom of a pool regardless of the pool's size.

Transition to Pascal's Principle by describing a closed, incompressible fluid system. Explain that because the fluid cannot be squashed, any change in pressure applied at one point is transmitted undiminished to every portion of the fluid and to the walls of the container. This is the 'mechanical lever' of the fluid world. Draw a hydraulic lift on the whiteboard: a small piston on one side and a large piston on the other. Walk through the logic that if P1 = P2, then F1/A1 must equal F2/A2. This shows that a small force on a small area can lift a massive weight on a large area. Explicitly address the conservation of energy here: remind students that while we gain force, we 'pay' for it in distance. The small piston must move much further than the large one rises. This prevents the misconception that we are getting 'free energy' from the fluid.

Conclude with a practice walkthrough focusing on total pressure versus gauge pressure. Many students forget to add the 1.01 x 10^5 Pascals of atmospheric pressure when calculating the 'total' pressure at the bottom of the ocean. Work through a mental model of a diver: why doesn't the massive weight of the ocean crush them instantly? The answer lies in internal pressure equalization. Finally, pose a quick scenario about a hydraulic jack: if the area ratio is 1:100, how much mass can a person lift by just leaning on the small handle? This reinforces the practical power of fluid mechanics before we move into buoyancy in the next session.

tasks: Calculate the total pressure at a given depth in the ocean.
Apply Pascal's principle to find the output force of a hydraulic lift.

sessions.title: Buoyancy
sessions.description: This session covers Archimedes' Principle and the concept of the buoyant force. You will learn how to determine if an object will sink or float based on density and displaced volume, which is vital for analyzing any system interacting with a liquid environment.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by drawing a connection between the previous discussion on fluid pressure and the concept of a net upward force. Most students intuitively understand that objects feel lighter in water, but the goal here is to transform that intuition into a rigorous mechanical analysis. Explain that buoyancy is not a new fundamental force, but rather the net result of pressure differentials: because pressure increases with depth, the upward force on the bottom of a submerged object is always greater than the downward force on its top. This 'upward push' is what we define as the buoyant force.

Transition into the formalization of Archimedes’ Principle. Instead of just stating the law, use a 'thought experiment' on the whiteboard: imagine a specific volume of water within a larger body of water. That volume is in equilibrium; therefore, the surrounding water must be supporting it with a force exactly equal to its weight. If we replace that 'water volume' with a solid object of the identical shape, the surrounding water still exerts that same upward force. This leads to the fundamental realization: the buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid displaced. This conceptual bridge is vital because it prevents the common mistake of thinking buoyancy depends on the object's mass or material; it depends solely on the volume of fluid the object pushes out of the way.

Now, address the mechanics of sinking versus floating by introducing the 'comparison of densities.' Draw a free-body diagram of an object in a fluid, showing gravity pulling down and buoyancy pushing up. Define the net force. If the object's density is greater than the fluid's, the weight exceeds the maximum possible buoyancy, leading to a downward acceleration. If the density is lower, the object will accelerate upward until it breaks the surface, reducing its displaced volume until the buoyant force exactly matches its weight. This is the moment to tackle the 'iceberg' problem. Guide the learners to see that for a floating object, the ratio of the submerged volume to total volume is exactly the ratio of the object's density to the fluid's density. This provides a clear mathematical tool for predicting how much of an object stays 'hidden' beneath the surface.

Conclude the session with a reality check on common misconceptions. Address the 'depth myth'—the idea that buoyancy increases as an object sinks deeper. Clarify that since liquids are nearly incompressible, their density remains constant, meaning the displaced weight (and thus the buoyant force) remains constant regardless of depth, provided the object doesn't crush. Use a quick practice prompt asking students to compare the buoyant force on a lead ball at 1 meter versus 10 meters deep. This ensures they separate the concept of 'total pressure' (which increases with depth) from 'pressure difference' (which remains constant across the object's height), reinforcing the core logic of the session before they move into dynamic fluid flow.

tasks: Calculate the buoyant force on a submerged block of wood.
Determine the fraction of an iceberg that remains submerged in seawater.

sessions.title: Fluid Flow and Bernoulli's Principle
sessions.description: This session introduces fluid dynamics through the Continuity Equation and Bernoulli’s Principle, which is essentially the conservation of energy for flowing fluids. You will be able to explain phenomena like lift and flow speed changes in pipes, expanding your mechanical toolkit to dynamic, non-rigid systems.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by shifting our perspective from 'static' fluids to fluids in motion. To keep the lecture grounded in the 'concept-first' style requested by the learner, we start by visualizing a steady stream of water through a pipe that changes size. The core question is: if the fluid is incompressible, where does the mass go? This leads us to the Continuity Equation. On the whiteboard, draw a pipe with a wide entrance and a narrow exit. By defining a volume element moving through these cross-sections over a small time interval, we derive A1v1 = A2v2. The most important takeaway here is the inverse relationship between area and velocity; it’s the 'crowd effect'—to move the same amount of people through a narrow hallway as a wide one, everyone has to run faster. A common pitfall for students is forgetting that this assumes a constant density, so emphasizing the 'incompressibility' of liquids like water is crucial for their mental model.

Once we establish that fluid speeds up in narrow regions, we transition to the 'why' using energy principles. This is where we derive Bernoulli’s Principle. Instead of presenting it as a magic formula, we treat it as an application of the Work-Energy Theorem. On the board, we track a segment of fluid and calculate the work done by pressure forces at both ends, the change in kinetic energy as the speed changes, and the change in potential energy due to height. By summing these, we arrive at the classic Bernoulli equation: P + 1/2ρv² + ρgh = constant. The central insight for the student must be that pressure is not just a 'push,' but a form of energy density. If kinetic energy goes up because the fluid is moving faster in a narrow pipe, the pressure must drop to conserve total energy.

To bridge theory and application, we introduce the Venturi Tube as a live 'whiteboard' problem. We ask the students to predict where the pressure is lowest based on the pipe's geometry. This often counter-intuitively challenges their basic instincts; many beginners assume that a narrow 'squeeze' increases pressure (confusing it with force or resistance). We use the practice task of calculating pressure differences to prove that the 'fast' fluid in the constriction actually has the 'lowest' pressure. This is a pivotal moment in the lecture because it explains the physical mechanism behind lift in aerodynamics and the suction in atomizers, transforming an abstract energy balance into a tangible tool for engineering.

We conclude by synthesizing these ideas into a holistic 'Fluid Mechanics' mindset. We discuss the limitations of our model—specifically that we are ignoring viscosity (internal friction) and turbulence—to prepare them for more advanced real-world physics. The final practice moment involves a 'sanity check' calculation: if the pipe's diameter doubles, what happens to the velocity and the pressure term? This ensures learners don't just plug numbers into the Bernoulli equation but actually perceive the quadratic relationship of the velocity term. This session effectively expands their Newtonian toolkit by showing that the same laws of motion and energy they used for blocks and pulleys apply just as rigorously to the flowing, invisible world of fluids.

tasks: Use the continuity equation to find the fluid speed in a constricted pipe.
Apply Bernoulli's equation to calculate the pressure difference in a venturi tube.

sessions.title: Waves as Coupled Oscillators
sessions.description: This session conceptualizes mechanical waves as a series of coupled oscillators passing energy through a medium. You will learn the relationship between wave speed, frequency, and wavelength, setting the stage for more advanced studies in acoustics and optics by viewing waves through the lens of Newtonian mechanics.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by framing a wave not as a new 'object,' but as a collective behavior of the systems we have already studied. Draw a series of masses connected by springs on the board. Explain that if we displace the first mass, the spring force acts on the second, then the third, and so on. This is the crucial bridge from Unit 5's previous focus on individual oscillators to the concept of a 'coupled' system. The key takeaway here is that a wave is energy in motion through a medium, while the medium itself only oscillates locally. This distinction prevents the common misconception that the 'air' or 'string' travels across the room with the signal.

Transition to the visualization of Transverse versus Longitudinal waves using this oscillator model. For transverse waves, draw the displacement of the 'masses' perpendicular to the line of the springs, creating the familiar sine wave profile. For longitudinal waves, visualize regions of 'compression' and 'rarefaction' where the masses move back and forth along the same axis as the energy travel. Use the 'slinky' analogy to help learners visualize that the density of the medium is what fluctuates in longitudinal waves, while the shape fluctuates in transverse ones. This setup is vital for understanding that the underlying Newtonian mechanics—F=ma and Hooke's Law—remain the same; only the geometry of the displacement changes.

Introduce the fundamental relationship between wave speed, frequency, and wavelength through a derivation of speed on a taut string. Start by drawing a small segment of a string under tension and show how the net vertical force (using small-angle approximations for sine) relates to the mass of that segment. By linking the tension to the restorative force and the linear mass density to inertia, derive why speed increases with tension but decreases with mass. This demonstrates that wave speed is a property of the medium, not the source. Explicitly address the error where students think making a sound 'louder' or 'higher pitch' makes it travel faster; clarify that only changing the 'stiffness' or 'heaviness' of the medium can do that.

Conclude by integrating the concept of energy transport. Explain that because each 'oscillator' in the chain is performing work on its neighbor, the wave is effectively a vehicle for kinetic and potential energy. Use a practice moment to have students calculate the speed of a wave on a specific string given its physical parameters. This exercise is designed to reveal if they understand that 'frequency' is determined by the source (how fast you shake the end) while 'speed' is determined by the string (how tight it is). End the session by hinting at how this mechanical view of waves provides the foundation for understanding everything from the sound of a violin to the transmission of light in later physics sequences.

tasks: Calculate the speed of a wave on a string given its tension and linear mass density.
Describe the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves using the oscillator model.
